The madness of Liverpool’s first foray into European competition

📅 15 Feb 2023 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2929 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thesefootballtimes

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, six-time European Cup winners; three-time UEFA Cup winners; a club synonymous with continental glory and famous nights under the floodlights: when it comes to European competition and experiences, you can safely say that Liverpool have been there, done that and bought many t-shirts.
  • It has been revealed that but every voyage begins with a first tentative step.
  • And while Liverpool dominated the pop scene, it also dominated the football world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, six-time European Cup winners; three-time UEFA Cup winners; a club synonymous with continental glory and famous nights under the floodlights: when it comes to European competition and experiences, you can safely say that Liverpool have been there, done that and bought many t-shirts. Few teams have as much history across the continent. Crazy nights in Istanbul, thundering roars against St-Étienne, and the despair of Heysel.

It has been revealed that but every voyage begins with a first tentative step. And for Liverpool, that initial journey into the great unknown commenced in the summer of 1964. The nation was gripped by Beatlemania as the Fab Four started to conquer the world. Such was the fervour, cinemas saw the release of A Hard Day’s Night accompanied by screaming teenagers while The Beatles’ return to their home city saw 300 people injured as around 150,000 attempted to see their idols in person. Liverpool became the epicentre of Britain, relegating London to a minor role – at least until the Swinging Sixties exploded into full flowering.

And while Liverpool dominated the pop scene, it also dominated the football world. Bill Shankly led Liverpool to the Second Division title in 1962, bringing the Reds back into the limelight. Incredibly, just two seasons later, Liverpool were English champions for the first time since 1947, powered by the goals of Roger Hunt, Ian St John and Alf Arrowsmith, who combined for 92 strikes that season.

That Championship was rewarded by Liverpool’s maiden entry onto the European stage – a place in the European Cup against the elite of the continent. It was a competition that, at the time, was still purely contested between league champions, a straight knockout from the beginning. No groups, no seeding.

It is almost impossible now to imagine Liverpool looking ahead to European competition as an unknown quantity, but it must be remembered that, until Shankly won that title in 1964, Liverpool had been in the doldrums.

Recent findings suggest that early British escapades into Europe were led by the likes of Wolves, Manchester United, Dundee and Hibs. As those clubs visited Barcelona, Madrid and Milan, Liverpool were mired in the Second Division, travelling to the slightly less glamourous metropolises of Scunthorpe, Plymouth and Rotherham. But all that had changed over the course of three seasons, and Liverpool were now playing alongside the giants of Europe.

The competition began with a preliminary round, although in effect it was basically a full round with only the previous season’s winners, Internazionale, afforded a bye. Given the straight draw and lack of seeding, Liverpool could theoretically have drawn anyone, including the likes of Real Madrid or Benfica – a potential recipe for a short-lived adventure.

But they managed to avoid the big boys and instead started their first European expedition with a trip to Iceland, whose champions were KR.

That season, KR became the first Icelandic team to enter the European Cup, so a trip to their island was uncommon in those days. And what a trip it was. Now there are probably direct flights from Liverpool to Iceland, but in those days it was somewhat more convoluted. Leaving from Liverpool, the team first had to travel to Manchester, then fly from Manchester to London, then fly from London to Prestwick, and finally from there on to Reykjavik.

What is more admirable is that some Liverpool supporters actually made the trip themselves. For many, with Liverpool having never been in Europe, this could have been their first trip outside of England. As one fan put it at the time, “We thought they were all eskimos,” before being surprised to find they were just like scousers. Different times, indeed.

In a recent development, ayrshire was also the home county of Shankly, so he couldn’t resist showing off the area to his boys before travelling on to Iceland. Full of pride, Shanks hired a bus to take the team to see … Butlin’s holiday camp. On proudly telling the camp leader that they were Liverpool FC, en route to Iceland, the gentleman helpfully told them, “I think you’ve taken the wrong road, sir.”.

In a recent development, and so, on 17 August 1964, Liverpool strode out for the very first time in European competition on the green grass of Reyjavik before 10,000 witnesses. Opening night nerves and a lack of experience affected them; at half-time, Liverpool were carrying a slim 1-0 advantage heading into the break. But then fitness levels and experience kicked in and two goals from Wallace and Hunt saw them run out 5-0 winners.

Industry observers note that A month later, the Icelanders made the long trip over to Anfield and, sadly for them, took another pasting, this time losing 6-1 with Ian St John grabbing a double. The competition was already down to just 16 teams and the draw for the first round proper awaited.

This time, Liverpool would not be getting such a straightforward tie. Fate threw them up against the Belgian champions, Anderlecht. This was an side that would then go on to win the following four Belgian First Division titles too – a streak that is still a national record.

In a recent development, it was a team led by the legendary Paul Van Himst, the scorer of 233 goals in 457 appearances for the club 16 seasons. This team was so good that when Belgium played against the Netherlands in 1964, there were ten Anderlecht players within the starting line-up. The only non-Anderlecht starter was the goalkeeper, Standard Leige’s Guy Delhasse, but he was substituted during the game by Jean-Marie Trappeniers who was, of course, an Anderlecht player. Liverpool had their work cut out.

It has been revealed that ahead of the game, Shankly decided on a rebranding of his team. Liverpool had traditionally played in red shirts and white shorts, but the manager decided that playing in all red would make the players look bigger and more intimidating – and so was born the legendary kit that we know and love so well today. Shankly was also aware of the threat posed by Van Himst and decided to throw a tough young defender up against him by the name of Tommy Smith.

And so onto Anfield for the first leg on 25 November. As the players were getting set to leave the changing room, Shankly gave them his final words of advice: “Right boys. You’ve nothing to beat tonight, they’re a load of rubbish.”.

Industry observers note that ninety minutes later, Liverpool had swept the Belgians aside 3-0, with goals from St John, Hunt and Ron Yeats. Shankly’s words on the Reds re-entering the changing room were plain: “Congratulations, you’ve just beaten one of the best teams in Europe.”.

A further 1-0 win in Brussels saw Liverpool through to the quarter-finals with four wins out of four under their belt. They seemed to be getting the hang of this European thing. But now some serious weeding out had been done and the competition was down to the major players, including the ever-dangerous trio of Real Madrid, Benfica and Inter. The hope would be to avoid one of those in the next round.

As luck would have it, Real Madrid drew Benfica, meaning one of those powers would be eliminated at this stage. Inter drew Scottish champions Rangers leaving Liverpool to face German champions Köln. It wasn’t the hardest tie but was far from the easiest either.

Köln had gained entry into the European Cup by becoming winners of the first-ever Bundesliga in 1963. A 0-0 stalemate in Germany was followed by the same back on Merseyside; 180 minutes of football and no goals to show for it. Back then, the next step was a playoff at a neutral venue.

Sources indicate that and so, on 25 March 1965, Liverpool and Köln fans met up at Feyenoord’s De Kuip for the decider. The Reds got off to a cracking start, with St. John tapping in from close range on 20 minutes followed by a Roger Hunt second on 37 minutes. Obviously the all-red strip was having the desired effect.

But Köln got back into the match through a Karl-Heinz Thielen header a minute later, meaning the Reds went into half-time 2-1 up. Shortly after kick-off, the Germans scored again, this time through Hannes Löhr, to level matters – and that is how the game remained until the final whistle.

So how do you decide a high-profile European Cup quarter-final when the playoff is tied? At the time, penalties were not in use, and so it came down to the ultimate test of football skills and composure – the coin toss. Unbelievable to think now but yes, a critical European Cup game would be decided on the flip of a coin. In the middle of the pitch. Televised.

Up stepped the captains, Ron Yeats and Hans Sturm. Under the floodlights, Yeats recalls the events wonderfully: “I thought, get in quick, I’ll have tails referee. And before he asked, he went yeah – Liverpool tails, Köln heads. Up it went and it come down and I couldn’t believe it, it stuck in a divot on its side. We were trying to blow over to tails by now and of course the German captain was trying to blow over to heads. And he had more puff than I had. It was coming over to heads and I stated to the referee, ref, you’re going to have to re-toss the coin. And he said you’re right Mr Yeats and he picked it up. I thought, great, up it went again.”.

Over 48,000 fans held their breath and waited for some sort of signal – and then the Liverpool players were jumping for joy. The Reds had just progressed to the semi-finals of the European Cup thanks to Yeats and tails.

According to recent reports, shankly went over to the Köln bench to commiserate, saying that it was no way to decide such a hard-fought, evenly-balanced game. And so, in their maiden continental odyssey, Liverpool found themselves in the European Cup semi-finals.

It has been revealed that joining them would be holders Inter, two-time champions Benfica, and ETO Győr, a Hungarian side who had just won the league for the first time. Probably hoping for Győr, Liverpool were instead drawn against Inter. If the Reds were hoping to get to the final in, appropriately enough, Milan, they were going to have to overcome Helenio Herrera’s men.

In a recent development, just how daunting a task would that be? Well, Il Grande Inter, as they would later be named in recognition of their prowess, had lifted the European Cup the year before, defeating the dominant Real Madrid 3-1. They were managed by perhaps the world’s most revered manager, Herrera, who had added steel through the adoption of a fifth defender, the libero, to elevate catenaccio to an art form.

It has been revealed that the team oozed quality: Sarti, Burgnich, Facchetti, Picchi, Corso, Mazzola, Suárez and Jair. They were on their way to recapturing the Scudetto, having just thrashed AC Milan 5-2. This definitely wasn’t Scunthorpe anymore.

Before that trip, however, Liverpool did have the small matter of an FA Cup final to contest against Don Revie’s Leeds. The crown jewel of the English season saw Liverpool lift the trophy after a 2-1 win, with all the goals in extra time. Wild celebrations followed back on Merseyside as the trophy was paraded before an estimated 250,000 people singing Beatles’ songs. For the first time in their history, the trophy sat within the halls of Anfield.

Sources indicate that just three days later, Liverpool welcomed Inter with players still suffering from an extra-time final on the spacious Wembley pitch and some lingering hangovers. Anticipation was at fever pitch with the ground full at 17.30 for an evening kick-off. Officially, 54,000 fans packed out Anfield, but there were probably more squeezed in.

In a recent development, if that wasn’t intimidating enough for Inter, Shankly then cranked up his mind games again. Wouldn’t it be a great idea if the FA Cup was paraded once again around the ground just before kick-off? And so it was, pitching the Liverpool fans into a state of pure rapture and upping the volume considerably. It was time for Liverpool to really see how they matched up against the great Inter.

Industry observers note that in a later interview, Ian St. John describes the game as “the night of nights”. Although at this point no-one knew how many great European Anfield nights the future would hold, this one would still go down alongside the best.

In a recent development, after just three minutes, a Callaghan cross was beautifully converted by Hunt. Mazzola then struck back shortly after for Inter, but after that it was all Liverpool. After 33 minutes, a lovely free-kick routine saw Callaghan dummy taking it, then run on as the free-kick was taken to get it back into his stride before hammering it into the corner. It was straight off the training ground. By now Anfield was a thundering cauldron of noise as Liverpool kept sweeping forward. A shell-shocked Inter staggered into the dressing room at half-time to attempt to catch their breath.

According to recent reports, after 74 minutes, a shot by Hunt was parried by Sarti straight into the path of St. John, who gratefully accepted the tap-in. It was job done on Merseyside. Liverpool had a two-goal advantage to take to Milan, meaning that the kings of catenaccio would have to come out of their shells. To this day, many older Liverpool fans will still swear that this Anfield night was the team’s greatest display and the club’s most atmospheric evening.

Ominously, the Italian press warned Liverpool that “you will never be allowed to win”. The shenanigans began as soon as the squad arrived at their Lake Como base. Church bells and singing locals ensured that sleep would be a luxury. And that was before the Reds had to step out in front of 76,000 at the San Siro. The game was going to need a firm and brave referee – and the man chosen for this significant night was one José María Ortiz de Mendíbil from Spain.

After eight minutes, Inter were awarded a free-kick just outside the area, which the Liverpool players believed was signalled as indirect by Ortiz. The referee strode out the ten yards for the wall, using the most exaggerated, extended strides you will ever see, before pushing the Liverpool wall back to what is more like 20 yards from the free-kick. Corso then struck a lovely shot into the corner – directly. A goal was awarded and Inter had just the start they needed.

Just two minutes later, things went from bad to worse. Inter forward Joaquín Peiró chased a long ball but Liverpool goalkeeper Tommy Lawrence was paying attention and got to it first. Bouncing the ball as he moved up the area, Lawrence was unaware of Peiró coming up behind him, who stole the ball on a bounce and rolled it into the empty net.

Recent findings suggest that the move represented what was generally viewed as “ungentlemanly conduct”, along with Peiró coming from an offside position, although I have to confess that it looked a fair enough steal to me. The Liverpool players protested vehemently but to no avail: Ortiz let it stand. Liverpool’s two-goal advantage was wiped out in the space of ten mad minutes.

Sources indicate that A third Inter goal by the glorious Facchetti after 62 minutes saw the Liverpool dream finally extinguished, even though St. John had a goal disallowed for an infringement unknown to him. The game ended 3-0 and Inter went on to reclaim the trophy in their own stadium against Benfica. The last image from that night in the San Siro was Yeats chasing Ortiz, calling him “El Bastardo” while kicking him on the ankles. It was a sad end to a glorious run.

According to recent reports, interestingly enough, the secretary of Inter at the time was Italo Allodi, who was later accused of match-fixing scandals including the infamous Juventus-Derby game in 1973. Allodi was close to a Hungarian called Dezső Solti who was accused by a referee in 1966 of trying to bribe him before the 1964 European Cup final with “enough dollars to buy five Mercedes”.

Recent findings suggest that later, UEFA and journalistic investigations found Solti guilty of offering bribes between 1963 and 1967. None of this proves that anything deliberately untoward was manifest that night, but suspicion lingers.

If skullduggery was indeed at work that night, the football gods made sure to rectify the situation going forwards. While Shankly would never win the European Cup, Bob Paisley, Joe Fagan, Rafa Benitez and Jurgen Klopp would see that Liverpool lifted ol’ significant ears six times, while Inter would only enjoy one more night of glory in 2010.

The 1964/65 European Cup campaign became the springboard for Liverpool’s dominance on the continent. They played in Europe for an incredible 20 successive seasons after their inaugural visit and still remain one of the most successful clubs in history. And it all started with a campaign that included visiting little-known Iceland, winning games through a twice-taken coin toss, and one of the greatest nights that Anfield has ever witnessed, before being curtailed in somewhat dubious circumstances. It taught Liverpool many lessons on the wily ways of European competition – lessons that they learned well and applied with a vengeance going forwards.

#96050. Brighton and Crystal Palace: the rise of a rivalry separated by 39 miles

Brighton and Crystal Palace: the rise of a rivalry separated by 39 miles

📅 26 Feb 2023 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3364 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thesefootballtimes

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Many bands have penned odes to their hometowns over time, singing the praises of their local streets and parks.
  • Sources indicate that however, when one considers David Bowie and his recollections of days gone by, it is safe to say that he did not enjoy such wistful memories.
  • Recent findings suggest that A touch harsh perhaps, but back in the 1970s and 1980s, Croydon did have a reputation as a concrete monstrosity, driven by London banning skyscrapers in the 1960s after which developers had to find somewhere to pour their concrete.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Many bands have penned odes to their hometowns over time, singing the praises of their local streets and parks. The Beatles waxed lyrical over Penny Lane and Strawberry Fields; The Kinks invited us to enjoy a Waterloo Sunset; while Gerry Rafferty took his saxophone to Baker Street. Each song echoed memories of great days and blissful childhoods.

Sources indicate that however, when one considers David Bowie and his recollections of days gone by, it is safe to say that he did not enjoy such wistful memories. When asked about how he would describe something dreary, he could only think of one place that summed it up for him: “It represented everything I didn’t want in my life, everything I wanted to get away from. I think it’s the most derogatory thing I can say about something: ‘God, it’s so fucking Croydon.”.

Recent findings suggest that A touch harsh perhaps, but back in the 1970s and 1980s, Croydon did have a reputation as a concrete monstrosity, driven by London banning skyscrapers in the 1960s after which developers had to find somewhere to pour their concrete. And hence the world of architecture was treated to such horrors as the Whitgift Centre, the NLA Tower, an underpass and a flyover.

In a recent development, oh, and if you think I am being unfair on Croydon town centre, I am speaking from a position of knowledge: I had to spend the first 16 years of my life meeting friends in the Whitgift Centre as the highlight after school. Trust me, the many ways to use concrete were richly celebrated there.

According to recent reports, but there did exist an escape route from the London suburb into pastures greener. On a sunny day, it was possible to pack the family up into a Ford Cortina and head off due south down the A23 across the scenic Sussex Downs until land ran out and you were in Brighton. In fact, the road was nicknamed the “Brighton Road” by locals.

Many a school trip was spent going down to that glorious seaside town, enjoying the delights of the pier, drinking too many fizzy drinks and then regretting it on the many fairground rides. A place of fine Victorian architecture, ice creams and sticks of rock. The yin to Croydon’s yang.

But the drive took a while. Croydon and Brighton are separated by 39 miles; even by train it takes almost an hour from East Croydon to Brighton. Again, I talk from experience having once fallen asleep travelling from Victoria to East Croydon and waking at 1am in Brighton – but let’s not get into that. The point is that the two cities are hardly next door and so really should have no reason to notice the other in any significant way.

In a recent development, it means that the football teams that exist in both towns, Crystal Palace and Brighton & Hove Albion, both have closer neighbours to concern themselves with. Palace especially, being in south London, have Wimbledon, Charlton and Millwall in their immediate vicinity, not to mention numerous possible other London derbies.

Brighton, meanwhile, are a little more isolated but Portsmouth is 42 miles away – similar to Croydon – and represents another south coast location. And so there should be no real rivalry, and certainly not enough for it to be called a derby in the same way as Liverpool and Everton or Manchester United and City.

It has been revealed that fans of both Palace and Brighton will happily tell you that it is not a derby in the true sense of the word, but a rivalry it most definitely is. For the reason why such a strange feud exists, one must go back to Tottenham in the 1960s.

Sources indicate that spurs during that time had a competent team, one that won the FA Cup in 1967, defeating rivals Chelsea 2-1. Playing alongside each other for Spurs on that day were two English midfielders, Alan Mullery and Terry Venables. While both played most of their days together at Tottenham, it wasn’t always a harmonious relationship, with Venables having to be second-in-command to Mullery as captain. They were not best of friends and so when both hung up their boots and started managerial careers, any future meetings between the two had the potential for sparks. And it wouldn’t be long before they would come face-to-face as rivals.

Sources indicate that the story moves on to 1970s. For many years, Palace and Brighton hadn’t even been in the same division together. That all changed during the 1974/75 season when they met in the third tier. Brighton had just gone through the short spell of leadership under Brian Clough who, having moved on to his ill-fated time at Leeds, had split with long-time partner Peter Taylor, who took over the reins.

At Palace, meanwhile, the colourful Malcolm Allison was in charge – a man to whom the words humility and shyness most definitely did not apply.

According to recent reports, the game at Brighton’s Goldstone Ground saw a higher-than-usual attendance and resulted in police arrests due to fighting between fans after reports of heavy drinking. The next season saw both teams fighting for promotion, which obviously heightened tensions somewhat, and the game at Selhurst Park saw Palace win 1-0 in front of their largest crowd for two years, despite what Allison described after as an overly physical approach from Brighton.

It is Allison who brings us nicely onto the theme of club nicknames. Until 1973, Crystal Palace had been known as The Glaziers in reference to the famous glass palace after which they are named. But Allison felt that this was not sexy enough, and so after glancing around Europe’s greatest sides and noting that Benfica were The Eagles, the nickname was changed to just that. Hence, a new terrace chant was born.

Brighton were known as The Dolphins, a name voted on by locals and reflecting the opening of a local Dolphinarium in 1969. But “Come on you Dolphins” just lacked a certain something. Therefore, when the sides met in 1976, a group of Brighton fans decided to answer Palace’s chants with “Come on you Seagulls” – a reference to their fine seaside setting. It was popular and soon became the official nickname, resulting in a fire sale of dolphin-themed merchandise on the south coast.

So now, Eagles vs Seagulls existed as a thing. But having rhyming birds as mascots hardly makes a rivalry. The game that saw the birth of the Seagulls also saw the game almost abandoned due to Palace fans throwing smoke bombs and other missiles onto the pitch. There was something starting to rumble.

According to recent reports, 1976 saw both sides eventually miss out on promotion, and both subsequently saw a change of management. Palace promoted Venables from coach following Allison’s resignation while Brighton gave Mullery his first managerial post. As such, promotion from the Third Division was a priority for both.

Sources indicate that despite their playing careers being well in the rear-view mirror, there was a simmering tension between the two ex-Spurs men, and their first meeting would occur at the Goldstone Ground, a game once again interrupted three times by smoke bombs. As if to add fuel to the fire, they drew each other in the first round of the FA Cup. The famous tale of ‘Challis of the Palace’ came into existence.

The initial tie was a draw, with Mullery complaining about Palace’s negative tactics, and the replay also drew a stalemate. As was the case in those days, a second replay was scheduled – and then postponed twice for weather before finally occurring at Stamford Bridge in early December – raising the tension. The Eagles took an early lead, which was then followed by a disallowed goal for Brighton when Peter Ward was adjudged to have handled. After the game, Jim Cannon admitted pushing Ward into the ball to cause the handball.

Industry observers note that and then came the moment that still lives in infamy between both sets of supporters. The Seagulls were awarded a penalty by referee Ron Challis after 78 minutes. Brian Horton converted but, to his astonishment, was forced to retake after Challis adjudged that a Brighton player had encroached, the player protesting that he had been pushed into the area by a Palace man. The second attempt was saved and Brighton ended up exiting the cup. Mullery was not best pleased.

Sources indicate that angry, he had to be escorted off the pitch by police while being heckled by Palace fans. According to his recollection, “A chap there [in the stands], I’d like to meet him again actually, he was up there and he poured a hot coffee all over my head. Literally I had about 30p in my pocket and looked up and remarked that’s about all you’re worth.”.

According to recent reports, finally losing his cool, he flicked V-signs at them, swearing at the same time, in an image that is famously revered by Brighton fans still to this day. The gesture ended up costing him more than 30p when the FA slapped him with a £100 fine.

The season ended on a high for both teams as they achieved promotion to Division Two, meaning that the simmering rivalry would continue. And both were on a roll: the 1978/79 campaign saw both clubs promoted together once again, this time to the massive time, with Palace snatching the title from Brighton in their final match. Their destinies seemed entwined at this time and it is really this whole period which created what some now call the A23 derby.

Since then, the rivalry has seen many infamous moments. 1982 saw Mullery appointed as Crystal Palace manager – a move that didn’t sit well with Palace fans (think Rafa Benitez at Everton). It didn’t help that he then oversaw two losses to Brighton which in part led to his dismissal two years later. Both sides slipped back to the Second Division, while a 1985 clash saw Brighton’s long-serving Irishman, Gerry Ryan, have his career ended by a tackle which broke his leg in three separate places.

In a recent development, four years later, one of the most famous – and indeed bizarre – games between the two took place. Their meeting at Selhurst Park saw referee Kelvin Morton in the thick of the action. It all started after about 16 minutes when Ian Wright scored a screamer of a goal for the Eagles, hitting it from the left wing over goalkeeper John Keeley when most were expecting a cross. Four minutes later, things went from bad to worse for Brighton as a nasty challenge by Mike Trusson on Palace’s Eddie McGoldrick saw him red-carded. Palace fans were enjoying the afternoon thus far.

Industry observers note that and then things started getting surreal. A high ball into the box saw Brighton defender Larry May seemingly strangle Mark Bright as he climbed for the header. Referee Morton had no hesitation in awarding a penalty. Bright himself took responsibility and powered it into the bottom corner. Two-nil to Palace and with an extra man.

Recent findings suggest that two minutes later, McGoldrick tormented the Brighton defence on the edge of the area before finally being cut down, resulting in a clear second penalty. Up stepped Bright again, but this time he was denied by a save from John Keeley, who diverted the ball away for a Palace corner.

It has been revealed that the corner was taken, the ball played around outside the area, before returning to a Palace player, who duly went down under a tackle and was awarded … another penalty. The crowd chanted for Wright to take responsibility, which he did – and duly hit the post.

According to recent reports, three penalties in three minutes: one scored and two missed. And we were still only in the first half.

Industry observers note that with that, the Eagles entered half-time 2-0 up and a man to the good but knowing that the game should have been dead and buried by now. The second half started off with the commentator’s sage words, “I am sure the referee is probably hoping he doesn’t have quite so many controversial decisions to make.” That wasn’t to be the case.

Just three minutes into the second half, a long kick from Keeley bounced into the Palace box; to much amazement, another penalty was awarded for what looked like an innocuous tussle. At least it was Brighton’s turn this time. The penalty was coolly put away by Alan Curbishley and suddenly the Seagulls were back in the game.

Recent findings suggest that eleven minutes then managed to pass without major incident before a cross aimed towards Wright was cut off by Brighton’s Ian Chapman, looking suspiciously like handball. Referee Morton felt so, awarding a fifth penalty, again to Palace.

By now everyone was confused as to who should take it. Bright had a record of scored one-missed one, while Wright had missed his effort. And so, John Pemberton was trusted with this fourth – a right-back who had never taken a penalty for Palace before – the reason becoming clear as he skied it over the bar.

In a recent development, five penalties across the space of 27 minutes – two converted and three missed. The rest of the game was relatively uneventful given all the preceding drama, leaving Palace with a useful 2-1 victory and memories for the fans to savour. To make it even sweeter for them, the Eagles gained promotion that season while Brighton remained in the second tier.

According to recent reports, the next 21 years saw the rivalry fade as Brighton suffered lower-league football and financial difficulties, resulting in only four meetings across that time. It is periods like this when fans suddenly realise that however much they may dislike each other, not having the friction active is worse. As one Palace fan nicely put it in an interview, “We are like two brothers that hate each other but love each other at the same time. A superhero needs a villain, and a villain needs a superhero. I think we need each other to make us realise how great football is and how much we love our teams.”.

It was only in the 2012/13 season when the rivalry sparked back into life. And, like the bizarre game discussed above with the five penalties, one of their clashes again caused jaws to drop.

The two sides met at the end of the season in a playoff semi-final in the Championship, with Brighton having finished fourth, one place above Palace – a two-legged meeting that would decide who could gain access to Premier League riches. The first leg was a damp squib, a goalless draw at Selhurst Park. But the second leg would see the strange occurrence of what became dubbed “Poo-gate”.

Sources indicate that as the Palace team entered their changing room ahead of the match, they were met with a disgusting odour from within. To their horror, the smell emanated from human excrement that had been smeared onto the toilet floor. The rivalry being what it is, there was immediate suspicion cast towards the source being someone of a Brighton persuasion, which if it was the case, just helped fuel Palace’s determination to gain revenge.

The players went out and defeated Brighton through two goals from Wilfred Zaha, thus eliminating them and gaining perceived justice. Considering how it may have driven the Palace players, Brighton manager Gus Poyet sent an angry email to the Brighton stadium staff demanding an explanation – shortly before then being suspended for a breach of contract.

The email famously stated, “For some reason that is still not clear to me, someone during the day had access to the away dressing room and done something terrible, trying to upset everyone related to Palace. To say it in clear English, someone had a poo all outside the toilets, over and around the toilets.”.

While the case of Poo-gate has rumbled on, a former Palace player has stated that the real cause was actually internal, stating that the Eagles coach driver that day had lost control of his bodily functions while rushing to the porcelain. Whether that is true or not, no-one can say. But it was a classic way to rekindle a dormant rivalry.

2018 saw the rivalry reignite once again in a spicy encounter. Brighton were home against Palace at Falmer Stadium and took an early lead through Glenn Murray. We should take a moment here to pause and talk about Murray, who has a close relationship with the Brighton-Palace dynamic.

In a recent development, his career really took off when he played for Brighton between 2008 and 2011, scoring 54 goals in 118 games. But then he shocked the Seagulls by signing for Palace, which was compounded by scoring against Brighton in a couple of meetings. However, he suffered a serious knee injury at the end of the 2013 season – where the opponent was, of course, Brighton.

According to recent reports, in 2015, he joined Bournemouth but from there was loaned on to the Seagulls, joining them for a second time. He later signed permanently, resulting in him facing his former club Palace once again in this 2018 tie. As stated, he gave them an early lead, but through what the Palace players saw as a very harsh penalty award.

Sources indicate that shortly after, Brighton claimed another penalty which was refuted. Palace players felt Brighton were guilty of play-acting and a melee broke out, during which Brighton defender Shane Duffy headbutted Palace defender Patrick van Aanholt. Brighton then went on to win 3-1 with ten men.

More recently, the Brighton-Palace games have been notable for late drama. A 2020 meeting saw Alexis MacAllister rescue a point for Brighton with a last-minute equaliser. The next game, in early 2021, saw Christian Benteke score a winning goal for Palace in stoppage time. The third game then saw Brighton rescue a point with a stoppage-time equalizer from Neal Maupay, leading to tense scenes with fans after the final whistle.

It has been revealed that as with any rivalry, there is an unwritten agreement between both sets of fans that they need each other to fuel excitement and that, deep down, it is really something that is primarily saved for the 90 minutes of competition for most. And a great example of this is the story of the Robert Eaton Memorial match.

Eaton was a Brighton fan who tragically lost his life during the Twin Towers attack of September 2001. A memorial fund was set up in his name to raise money for youth sports clubs across the world and fans of both teams decided to raise money for it by hosting an annual game between them.

Supported by the two clubs, games have been held in various locations and have included ex-professionals such as Peter Ward, Ricky Marlow, Simon Rodger, Peter Taylor and Paul Rogers. Ten of thousands of pounds have been raised and, despite some occasional spicy challenges, great enjoyment has been had by all for a great cause. As one fan commented, the game represents “a kind of Christmas Day truce.”.

It has been revealed that and so, the Eagles vs the Seagulls all really stemmed from the mid-70s. Unlike a true derby, it developed due to managerial personalities and both clubs being often linked in promotion battles. While the 70s was the true birthplace, it has since continued as generations of fans pass down the rivalry from parent to child.

There are probably many current fans of both teams who don’t know the origin story and may well not care – to them it is just something they have always taken for granted: cats chase mice, dogs chase cats and Palace don’t like Brighton. But it is interesting to see how friction can develop from almost 50-year-old origins. While it may not have the status of Arsenal-Tottenham or Aston Villa-Birmingham, to both sets of fans it represents the biggest league game of the season.

#96049. Man for Man: How Brighton’s Press Suffocated Arsenal

📅 23 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3237 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Spielverlagerung ↗ Open Full Page

Man for Man: How Brighton’s Press Suffocated Arsenal

📅 23 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3237 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Spielverlagerung

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • von Next Generation am 23.09.2026 in den Kategorien Premier League,Uncategorized mit 0 Kommentaren.
  • BrBrighton arrived at the match fresh off a 3–2 win at Old Trafford, while Arsenal boasted a clean defensive record and a reputation for controlling games and seeing them out like few other teams in Europe.
  • In a recent development, arteta’s Arsenal are among the best sides in Europe at controlling games out of possession.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

von Next Generation am 23.09.2026 in den Kategorien Premier League,Uncategorized mit 0 Kommentaren.

BrBrighton arrived at the match fresh off a 3–2 win at Old Trafford, while Arsenal boasted a clean defensive record and a reputation for controlling games and seeing them out like few other teams in Europe. The match ended 3–0, sparking immense hype around Brighton’s pressing. This analysis explores the underlying mechanisms: their man-oriented pressing across the entire pitch, their asymmetrical build-up play, their transition behavior after winning the ball, and the three goals themselves.

In a recent development, arteta’s Arsenal are among the best sides in Europe at controlling games out of possession. Any opponent who sets out to establish order is playing on the ground Arsenal own. Hürzeler therefore decided against control – not control surrendered in the sense of a low block, but a chaotic game state that Brighton generated themselves and were therefore prepared for.

System & movement with the ball – FC Arsenal.

System & movement with the ball – Brighton & Hove Albion.

According to recent reports, the thread running through ninety minutes: Arsenal were not to settle into an organised phase either with or without the ball. Three decisions delivered that. The build-up was set up asymmetrically – on the right Brighton prepared the long ball and occupied the landing zone before it was played, on the left counter-movements opened the short route. It was never long instead of short, but two prepared options that would have demanded opposite answers from Arsenal. After regains the ball was not secured but risked immediately, because a secured ball gives the opponent exactly the seconds they need to reorganise. And the press lived off intensity and constantly newly introduced starting points: when a line was played through, Brighton did not stand still but re-established their shape and triggered again.

Recent findings suggest that all three decisions give up ball control in the classical sense. Control came instead from preparation – if you know where the ball will land and you are standing there beforehand, you control the situation without the ball.

Industry observers note that what followed can be pinned to a single number: 41 Arsenal turnovers in their own danger zone. That is not a figure a side of this quality produces because they play badly, but because they never reached the game state their build-up is designed for.

Brightons manorientated press against a 4-3-3.

According to recent reports, the press was simple in principle and demanding in execution. Brighton set up with man-reference to their direct opponent and switched into pure man-marking on the trigger. Against a side that tracks from the first second, marking assignments can be pulled apart by movement before any pressure exists; Brighton refused to offer that, because their shape stayed compact until the trigger moment.

In the “mid-block,” positioned +1 on the last line, but ready at any moment to transition into a high press upon a pressing trigger.

In a recent development, the steering began with Ayari. He curved his pressing run so that Konsa stayed in his cover shadow and Raya was forced to the other side. Kostoulas marked Gabriel, while Chema Andrés and Groß pushed aggressively onto Arsenal’s No. 8s. Groß in particular tracked the dropping Rice and at times advanced into the first pressing line, in some sequences all the way onto Konsa. That requires Rice to be picked up by a team-mate in the same moment – the man-marking worked through handovers as much as through tracking. Centrally, the striker and the No. 10 rotated accordingly: whoever had the shorter route to the next man on the ball pushed out, while the other covered behind him and took over again on the next trigger.

Recent findings suggest that it only held up because the centre-backs came with it. Vušković and Struijk stepped out onto Ødegaard and the dropping Havertz and prevented an underload in central areas. When Arsenal built with three in the first line, Brighton kept one centre-back zonal in the back line – but with permanent reference to the unmarked player in the No. 6 space, stepping onto him the moment the press was triggered. Arsenal’s numerical advantage in build-up therefore never translated into a free man anywhere on the pitch.

Raya was part of the marking scheme too. Ayari’s cover shadow left only the route through a No. 6, and under man-marking that is not an escape but a duel that begins with the first touch. Raya’s body shape reinforced it: he tended to open only half-way, which effectively removed the switch to the far side from his repertoire. Steered onto his right foot, only the right-hand build-up side remained; the left lay open for long stretches and was unreachable for the one player who could have found it.

Every back pass served as a trigger. When the ball went back to Raya or the centre-backs, Brighton pushed up as a unit and raised the defensive line. The density around the ball came less from the base shape than from the recovery runs: players who had been beaten sprinted back, and they did not run at the ball but with a cover shadow onto the lay-off option behind it. An Arsenal player with a marker in his back therefore had neither the lay-off nor the chance to turn.

Sources indicate that this is precisely where Brighton differed from most sides who get played through against Arsenal. The usual response is to stay deep once a line has been broken and wait for the shape to settle. Brighton instead pushed up into the next line and used the mid-block to prepare the next jump back into the high press – even when that press had just been beaten. The press therefore had not one starting point per possession, but a steady supply of new ones, and Arsenal had to solve the same pressure several times within a single attack.

Arsenal’s core problem was the absence of a threat in behind. Their attempts to play through the press came without pace beyond the back line, so Brighton were never forced to turn towards their own goal. That made the press cheap: no threat in behind, therefore no need to drop the line. There are three answers to committed man-marking – movement that drags your own marker away and opens space for a third player, a dribble that beats the assignment one-on-one, or a target man who wins the long balls. Arsenal produced none of them.

When the high press was beaten, Brighton dropped into a 5-1-4 and inverted the priority. The five in the last line formed a deliberate overload against Arsenal’s front line – in exactly the moment a man-oriented side is most vulnerable, because its players are facing forward while the opponents are already moving. Brighton took the depth out of the situation first and only then thought about the ball again.

A “mid-block” in a 5-1-4 formation. The foremost players protected the “red zone” by using their cover shadows and shifting extremely compactly. Arsenal was mostly forced to play around the block, repeatedly giving Brighton time to reorganize.

A single No. 6 held the connection in front, while the four most advanced players stayed narrow and closed the centre with cover shadows rather than pressing the ball carrier. Arsenal found no central switch on the ball-near side and had to play around the block. Every trip around it cost seconds that Brighton used to shift across, so the end of the route offered the same congestion as the start. In some phases six players stood in the last line.

The block was not a terminus. At every Arsenal back pass Brighton jumped out again and restarted the high press – the same trigger as in the high phase, only from a deeper starting position. The spare man in the last line made that possible, usually Vušković: because the overload left him without a fixed opponent, he could step out, cover the depth and pick up a man himself a moment later. That freed a midfielder to push forward without leaving an assignment open behind him – precisely the point at which sides with a similar approach usually come apart.

According to recent reports, in the “mid-block” phase, the “+1” players organized themselves to execute early handovers and jump into pressing situations. Here, Vuskovic—acting as the “+1” player from the defensive line—steps up to pick up the Arsenal player operating in the number 10 position.

According to recent reports, on top of that came the trap on the touchline. Once Brighton steered the ball wide, players jumped in from every direction: the ball-near winger closed the route back, the No. 6 covered inside, the back line stepped out. The back pass, the switch and the ball in behind did not disappear one after another but at the same time. Take away only the back pass and a side switches play; take away only the switch and they play backwards and start again. When all that remains is an individual action against several opponents with the touchline at your back, it almost always ends with the opposition.

Sources indicate that after a regain there are two basic options: risk the ball immediately to launch the attack, or secure it to establish order. Hürzeler consistently chose the first, and it follows directly from the overall idea – a secured ball would have given Arsenal exactly the seconds in which their structure reorganises.

When a high press was bypassed, Brighton succeeded in forcing Arsenal into congested situations in the area in front of the back four. In doing so, the players who had been bypassed shifted to block the passing lanes of the players positioned behind the ball. This created additional pressure on the ball carrier, who was simultaneously facing pressure from the front via a “negative” pressing movement (i.e., pressing towards their own goal).

Sources indicate that the counter was prepared before the regain. When Arsenal found a player in the No. 6 space after beating the press, Brighton immediately closed his back pass, so the turnover inevitably occurred in a moment when Arsenal were all ahead of the ball. The density around the ball, a defensive necessity, meant in attack that Brighton were central and therefore on the shortest route to goal. The first ball went to the deepest player, followed by a dribble at speed into the box, with no intermediate step and no square pass for safety.

Recent findings suggest that in the build-up phase, Brighton utilized a diamond shape. De Cuyper and Boscagli engaged in a 2v2 duel on the left flank, while Kostoulas, Gomez, and Kadioglu created a high 3v3 situation on the right. Briefly, both center-backs and a defensive midfielder would spread out to widen the formation. Additional support occasionally came from Groß, dropping back from the number 10 position. Ayari occupied Konsa and Gabriel through constant runs into the open spaces ahead of him.

Industry observers note that in deep build-up Brighton baited Arsenal in deliberately. Verbruggen put his foot on the ball while the centre-backs split and lengthened the pressing runs of their opponents. On paper that produced a 3v2 against Arsenal’s first line – except Hürzeler had no intention of playing through that overload on the ground. 25 of 40 goalkeeper passes were long, 62.5 per cent, and they went overwhelmingly to the right.

Industry observers note that the structure allowed for a long ball to the right flank, feeding into the 3-3 formation. This created opportunities to contest the second ball or flick on the aerial pass. Additionally, Vuskovic offered a short, low passing option as the free player.

It has been revealed that there, Brighton consistently created a 3v3 – an intact structure for the second ball regardless of whether the first contact was won. That is exactly what separates it from an ordinary long ball: the action was not judged by the aerial duel but by the situation that followed it. Kostoulas dropping added to the disorganisation of Arsenal’s high line, because a centre-back had to decide whether to follow him between the lines or let him turn. After winning second balls Brighton played on at high speed and looked for an early shot or an early cross, even against a defensive overload – again the decision for tempo over the clean attack.

In a recent development, once again, the 3-3 structure on the right flank. Here, from open play.

Recent findings suggest that on the left Brighton worked through pinning rather than through length. Boscagli stepping inside dragged Saka into central areas and took him out of the wide zone Arsenal needed him in defensively, while De Cuyper dropped and offered the mid-range diagonal once the assignments had been pulled apart. The asymmetry was a personnel decision: the players for second balls were on the right, the players who could drag markers out of position on the left. Arsenal would have had to condense against one side and hand over assignments cleanly against the other.

The team’s build-up play was asymmetrical, featuring a high, wide approach on the right contrasted with the left flank: Boscagli often played an inverted role—supplementing the existing diamond formation—which opened up space for de Cuyper. Meanwhile, Groß and Kostoulas occupied the players on Arsenal’s right defensive flank, enabling Brighton to find low-ball solutions against the press.

Sources indicate that with the ball in midfield there were two patterns. The first was the deliberate back pass to Verbruggen to pull Arsenal’s block out, followed by the same long-short structure as in deep build-up. The back pass was not a safety option here but the tool that created the space behind the pressing line in the first place.

According to recent reports, the second pattern worked through central and wide tension at high speed, supplemented by rotations within their own structure. Arsenal repeatedly failed to hand over their pressing assignments in a coordinated way against it – the same weakness Brighton had solved cleanly in their own press. In possession Brighton’s shape approached a 4-3-3: Chema Andrés as the deepest No. 6, Groß with freedom from the left half-space, Kadıoğlu pushing up early to support Gómez, Boscagli starting slightly deeper on the left.

The 1-0 by Groß in the 31st minute is the whole strategy in one sequence. Brighton play back to the goalkeeper from midfield, go long, lose the first contact and win the second ball. After a phase of circulation the next attack meets a back line that has already been destabilised: Kostoulas drops, Arsenal’s midfield and Konsa step out, and Kostoulas lays the ball back against the direction of the pressure to Groß. Because Ayari runs in behind at the same time, Arsenal’s defenders drop – and Groß has the time for the shot from around 20 metres. In the build-up Brighton had used rotations to drag Guimarães over to the left.

Industry observers note that the opening goal stems from a positional attack. Kostoulas spots open space and makes a run into it. With a pass played across his standing leg, he feeds the ball to Groß in the space between the lines. As Groß takes a few quick touches and dribbles toward the defensive line, Gabriel and Calafiori drop back together, thereby opening up a shooting lane.

The 2-0 by Kostoulas shortly before half-time follows the same logic from the opposite direction. After a set piece of their own, Brighton clear an Arsenal counter and transition again immediately, 4v5 in Arsenal’s half, and once more the shot comes from distance while the centre-backs drop off.

Much like the goal that made it 1–0, both defenders went to ground near the ball carrier, thereby opening up space for the goalscorer—this time arising from a transition situation.

Both goals share the same cause: Arsenal’s centre-backs stepped out too late to press the man between the lines. React only when the shooting motion starts and you cannot get into the block from 20 to 25 metres. What is striking is that this passivity is the same one Arsenal revealed in their own build-up – a side that does not leave its position to offer itself does not leave it to close down a shooter either.

The 3-0 by Chema Andrés came from a corner: Groß delivered from the left, Brighton had created an overload at the far post and protected it with two blocks, and Chema rose completely unmarked to head in off the inside of the post.

In a recent development, two goals up, many sides would have defended deeper. Brighton came out with unchanged and at times higher pressing intensity, and the coordination was visibly drilled: marking assignments were swapped cleanly even in dynamic situations, and Arsenal’s structural adjustments were absorbed.

Industry observers note that arsenal had managed a few organised possession phases in Brighton’s half in the first period; in the second it became harder. In those phases they built with a back three, Rice as the third centre-back, Ødegaard dropping alongside Guimarães and the full-backs occupying the half-spaces. Arteta reacted around the hour: Zubimendi and Merino for Timber and Guimarães, with Rice moving to right-back, followed shortly by Gyökeres and Eze for Ødegaard and Tzolis. There was no noticeable effect, because the problem did not lie in the shape but in the assignments in front of it.

There was also a layer that usually goes missing in analysis: Brighton used tactical fouls deliberately to stop Arsenal finding a rhythm. Arteta admitted afterwards that the game had been “very difficult to control”, pointing to lost first and second balls and to Brighton’s directness.

Industry observers note that arteta’s Arsenal being outplayed this clearly is rare. That it happened proactively and aggressively is rarer still – most sides who take something from Arsenal do it with a low block and efficiency. Hürzeler deliberately stepped back afterwards and praised his players’ courage, which gets to the heart of it: the proposal only works if eleven players are willing to carry it through in every single sequence.

According to recent reports, the interesting question is where the idea came from. Chelsea were a common opponent: Brighton had 74 per cent possession there and lost 3-4 against a counter-attacking side – control right down to the numbers, without return. Alonso’s Chelsea tried the opposite route against Arsenal, a deliberate surrender of control, also without success. The likely derivation lies between the two: neither give up control nor chase it, but generate the unsettled game state yourself and be prepared for it.

In a recent development, there is no reason for panic at Arsenal, but Arteta will need answers against a high press. The build-up was predictable for long stretches, and above all the direct option with pace in behind was missing as a threat. As long as that does not exist, a man-oriented press costs very little against this side.

Sources indicate that for Brighton the open question is repeatability. Man-marking of this commitment, collective recovery runs with cover shadows and a touchline trap that requires everyone to trigger at once are hard to produce twice in an English week. Whether the plan works was answered on this afternoon. How often it can be produced will decide the season.

LC can often be found in the classroom, preferably on the soccer field, and—on rare occasions—on LinkedIn.

Chelsea are great entertainers but possess clear weakness

📅 30 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 24 min read (4880 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~24 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Chelsea are promising to be this season’s Premier League entertainers and yet manager Xabi Alonso seemingly believes less is more when it comes to possession.
  • In a recent development, alonso has started with two wins from two league games in charge of Chelsea, with his team scoring seven goals and conceding five.
  • But perhaps the most significant numbers are around how much – or how little – Chelsea are having the ball.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chelsea are promising to be this season’s Premier League entertainers and yet manager Xabi Alonso seemingly believes less is more when it comes to possession.

In a recent development, alonso has started with two wins from two league games in charge of Chelsea, with his team scoring seven goals and conceding five. So far, it has been a lot of fun – if not entirely convincing.

But perhaps the most significant numbers are around how much – or how little – Chelsea are having the ball. Having finished their 3-2 victory over Fulham with 38.11 per cent of possession, Chelsea had just 25.6 per cent in the 4-3 success over Brighton and Hove Albion and successfully completed 146 passes. Both were their lowest figures on record in the Premier League.

“The data is not important,” Alonso said. “It’s how you play and what we can do better. I don’t say ‘today we need to have 60 per cent or 20 per cent’. I never talk about those things. It’s about how to prepare, how to be more competitive.”.

Chelsea’s third goal against Brighton, scored in the 32nd minute, best summed up the London club under Alonso to date. It took the home side three passes to go from the edge of their own penalty area to João Pedro scoring against his former club.

Jorrel Hato passed the ball to Morgan Rogers, he then released Hato down the left and the wing-back slid the ball across for João Pedro to finish. It was a devastating counter-attack and should have put Chelsea on course for a much easier win.

Joao Pedro finishes off a deadly Chelsea counter-attack and gives the Blues a 3-0 lead 🔥 pic.twitter.com/wAr0ckIgXJ.

It has been revealed that “After 30 minutes, we are 3-0 and probably, in that moment, we have played too much the result,” Alonso stated. “It’s quite normal, it happens in many teams. I am sure in the future we can manage it better.”.

Industry observers note that it is one thing outscoring Fulham and a depleted Brighton team without having the ball, but can Chelsea do that against the bigger and better teams? We will get an early indicator in the next game against Arsenal at the Emirates.

Alonso’s approach has some similarities to the way in which Antonio Conte set up his Chelsea title-winning team. Just as Conte converted Victor Moses into an effective right wing-back, Alonso started Pedro Neto there on Sunday.

After Roméo Lavia had opened the scoring, it was Neto who grabbed Chelsea’s second goal against Brighton by drifting into the penalty area to finish from Rogers’s low cross.

"It's a nightmare for the goalkeeper!"Bart Verbruggen and Mats Wieffer's collision leads to Romeo Lavia scoring his first goal for Chelsea ⚽️ pic.twitter.com/q5awbdwVV0.

"Pedro Neto Pounces!"Morgan Rogers goes past his defender before sliding the ball across to Neto! 💥 pic.twitter.com/WHZCIGsOLl.

But whereas Conte’s team gave up little at the back, Alonso’s Chelsea are yet to balance their effective transitional play with shutting out their opponents.

Neto was partly to blame for Brighton’s first goal, as he missed a challenge in the build-up to Malick Yalcouyé’s brilliant volley. Making his Chelsea debut, goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez could do nothing to stop it and can expect to be kept busy this season if things do not change.

“I have come here to challenge and to try and win the Premier League,” Martínez stated. “I know the talent we have up front. I try to bring that solidity at the back.”.

"Yalcouye with a sumptuous volley!"Malick Yalcouye puts Brighton on the scoreboard with a venomous volley 😳 pic.twitter.com/8UeeyvPjUw.

Conte’s Chelsea had N’Golo Kanté to mop up in midfield and that is an area of the pitch that is causing Alonso some difficulties. Manchester City target Enzo Fernández was once again left out of the squad and Moisés Caicedo was not deemed fit enough to start.

In a recent development, caicedo was eventually thrown on when Chelsea were trying to stop Brighton completing a remarkable comeback, but he was quickly forced off again with an injury. The club have been exploring a move for Monaco midfielder Lamine Camara and that need looks even more pressing now.

It has been revealed that “We want the best for the team and that’s why we took a decision [on Fernández] against Luton and today,” Alonso stated. “What’s going to develop? We’re not sure. We can prepare. We are preparing for all the scenarios. But I assure you that whatever happens, from Wednesday [when the transfer window is shut] we’ll have a good enough squad to compete in all the Premier League games.”.

Chelsea’s new set-piece coach Austin MacPhee had celebrated Lavia’s goal, which came partly as a result of a corner but owed more to a mistake from Brighton goalkeeper Bart Verbruggen.

MacPhee, however, will not have liked Brighton’s second-half goals. It was from a short corner that the visitors managed to work the ball to Pascal Gross and his cross was diverted into his own net by João Pedro.

Joao Pedro puts Pascal Groß's cross into his own net and Brighton have brought it back to 3-2 👀 pic.twitter.com/maBMwVu3DC.

Gross’s headed third goal also came at the end of a set-piece, but, fortunately for Chelsea, it was in the sixth minute of added time and Cole Palmer had already made the points safe for the home team before then.

Palmer had done little to impress watching England head coach Thomas Tuchel until he picked up the ball in the 74th minute, shrugged off two Brighton challenges and produced a brilliant finish to beat Verbruggen.

Cole Palmer finishes EXPERTLY to give Chelsea their two-goal cushion back 💥 pic.twitter.com/6xI9W8xe2q.

Fabian Hürzeler, the Brighton manager, stated his team “dominated” the game, but acknowledged: “I think if you spend so much money on these kinds of players, like Rogers, Palmer or João [Pedro], then, of course, a team like Chelsea can rely on this individual quality. And they showed it in certain moments of the game.”.

Palmer, João Pedro and Rogers are clearly going to be a huge problem for Chelsea’s opponents. But Alonso’s team cannot rely on having to score three or four goals to win games. And they might need to have a bit more of the ball.

"The game today was a special game for me." João Pedro says he was happy with his performance for Chelsea against Brighton 🔵 pic.twitter.com/fWSqWo7ert.

Recent findings suggest that 6 - João Pedro today was the sixth player (and first for Chelsea) to score a goal, assist a goal, and score an own goal in the same Premier League game, and first since Tottenham Hotspur's Son Heung-min against Man City in December 2023.Eventful. pic.twitter.com/xRVjqkOY9D.

There have already been three goals in the first half at Stamford Bridge but it is still goalless at Elland Road and the Stadium of Light in the other two 2pm kick-offs.

According to recent reports, the Brighton fans have been singing ‘The Falklands are ours’ at Chelsea’s Argentine substitute Valentin Barco. The Brighton fans had also been giving the club’s former striker Joao Pedro some stick. Pedro celebrated his goal right in front of them. Touche.

The Brazilian missed a sitter earlier but he makes no mistake this time and goes to celebrate in front of the travelling Brighton fans. Pedro owes a lot of gratitude from Hato, who drives down Chelsea’s left from inside his own half to the edge of the Brighton box.
