Latest Update: Rio, 1989: Chilean skullduggery, hidden razor blades and Brazilian flares

📅 07 Mar 2023 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3041 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thesefootballtimes

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the word “skullduggery” is defined as “underhanded or unscrupulous behaviour; trickery”.
  • Sources indicate that it should never be a surprise the lengths teams will go to in order to win.
  • Sources indicate that to this day, Brazil hold the amazing record of having qualified for every World Cup finals tournament.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the word “skullduggery” is defined as “underhanded or unscrupulous behaviour; trickery”. It has been intertwined with football since time immemorial, exhibited in various degrees. It has been employed by the greats, not least Diego Maradona, and in recent times by compatriot Emiliano Martinez. Players have been banned from tournaments following drug tests and Serie A has been peppered by various instances of a dubious nature. Even the Brazilians are not exempt from employing it, as demonstrated by Rivaldo during the 2002 World Cup.

Sources indicate that it should never be a surprise the lengths teams will go to in order to win. And yet it still does. Indeed, the story of Brazil’s 1989 World Cup qualifying campaign involved a classic example of the win-at-all-costs mentality. Sometimes truth is stranger than fiction.

Sources indicate that to this day, Brazil hold the amazing record of having qualified for every World Cup finals tournament. They have hosted the tournament twice, but on all other occasions they got through the CONMEBOL qualification process to reach the finals. To imagine them getting eliminated at that stage is almost too much to consider. After all, how do you stop a team like Brazil when you are a smaller South American nation?

In the 1980s, Brazil enjoyed a generation of incredible talent, highlighted by the famous 1982 team containing the likes of Zico, Socrates, Falcao and Eder. Playing attacking football, they charmed the world before becoming unstuck against the Italians on an infamous night in Barcelona.

In a recent development, the loss brought about a period of introspection for the Selecao as they wrestled with balancing their natural attacking game with a more pragmatic European approach to avoid another 1982. Going into the 1986 World Cup, their style changed slightly, with more defensive steel added. They still had a team containing superb strikers such as Careca and Muller, but Zico was 33, Socrates was 32 and Falcao was the same. The 1982 generation was fading from the picture.

Mexico 86 again saw Brazil eliminated by European opposition – this time in the shape of a France team that was also starting to see the end of a golden generation.

Recent findings suggest that qualification for the 1990 World Cup saw Brazil up against Chile and Venezuela in a three-team round-robin. It was one of three CONMEBOL qualification groups from which the two top teams with the best records would automatically qualify for Italia 90 while the third top team would playoff against a side from the OFC section.

Venezuela had a relatively weak squad and so the group would come down to Chile and Brazil; how they would perform against each other and what goal difference they could rack up against the Venezuelans.

Sources indicate that both teams travelled to Caracas a week apart to start their campaigns, and both came away with comprehensive victories, Brazil 4-0 and Chile 3-1. Brazil’s victory included two goals from Bebeto and one from Romario – a deadly partnership that was beginning to click. That set the stage for the first meeting between the two, which took place in Santiago in August 1989. A win for either team would place them in pole position to win the group.

Tension was high ahead of kick-off. With the game delayed by 15 minutes, the referee insisting on moving back photographers, Romario and defender Alejandro Hisis exchanged words. The striker took offence to something said, Branco having to pull him away before things further.

In a recent development, within two minutes, the game erupted: Chile could have been down to ten men following a vicious knee-high tackle on Branco by midfielder Raul Ormeno. As Branco was led to the side of the pitch for treatment, a roar from the crowd drew attention to Romario. It appeared that he and Hisis were still feuding, and the camera revealed Romario being followed by three Chileans while Hisis lay on the ground.

Sources indicate that the referee showed the PSV striker a straight red and Brazil faced 86 minutes a man short. If anyone wasn’t sure of what exactly had occurred, Romario cleared up the situation after the game: “I didn’t hit him that hard.”.

It has been revealed that chile didn’t enjoy a one-man advantage for long. Fourteen minutes into the game Ormeno, who was clearly pumped up, lost the ball to Valdo and brought him down. Immediately realising the consequences, he tried desperately to persuade referee Diaz Palacio to keep his cards in his pocket. It was to no avail. A second yellow card was produced and the Chilean crowd howled as Ormeno had to be escorted off by four teammates. The first half was only a third of the way in.

Industry observers note that scoreless at half-time, Brazil took the lead in the second half through an unfortunate own goal from Hugo Gonzalez. As the game stretched on, it appeared as if Brazil were going to leave Chile with a crucial away victory. But, with just nine minutes remaining, La Roja struck back through a bizarre goal from Ivo Basay.

According to recent reports, brazilian goalkeeper Taffarel had the ball in his area when the referee suddenly decided that he had held it for too long and awarded an indirect free-kick to Chile just four yards from the goal. The quickest Chilean player to react was Jorge Aravena, who touched the ball to Basay to convert.

Brazil were stunned. Chilean fans celebrated on the edge of the pitch, while the Brazilian technical staff went ballistic. There was confusion in every direction but, at the end of 90 minutes, the honours were even, little dividing the two countries in the standings. Brazil were marginally in front on goal difference.

The following week saw O Selecao host Venezuela in Sao Paulo and dish out another lesson, running out 6-0 victors thanks to four goals from Careca, proving that Brazil still had three fearsome strikers to choose from. Seven days later, it was Chile’s turn to host Venezuela and, like the week before, Venezuela were again on the receiving end of a thrashing, this time going down 5-0.

Only one game remained: Brazil against Chile in the Maracana on 3 September 1989. Both teams had two wins and a draw but Brazil’s goal difference was three better than Chile’s. If La Roja were going to eliminate their mighty neighbours and head to Italia 90, they needed to win in Rio. It would be a tough ask, but at least they were in a position where it was a possibility.

Get an early goal and maybe the Brazilians would start to tense up in front of an expectant crowd. And let’s not forget that Brazil had suffered unexpected heartache at the Maracana before, losing the 1950 final to Uruguay. It was game on for that World Cup berth. But the Selecao had also never lost a World Cup qualification game in its history.

Recent findings suggest that in front of a huge crowd of over 140,000, the two sides took to the pitch. Brazil would be without Romario – still suspended following the previous meeting’s sending-off – but with Careca and Bebeto upfront, they looked strong. Unfortunately for Chile, they would be without star striker Ivan Zamorano, who was unable to make it back from his Swiss side, Neuchatel Xamax, in time. The game was going to require an experienced referee, which it got in the shape of Argentine Juan Carlos Loustau.

The last time Chile had beaten Brazil was a famous 4-0 win during the 1987 Copa America, and many of the team were in this side. Unsurprisingly, given the stakes, the early minutes were once again physical. Chilean left-back Hector Puebla left his studs on the knee of Mauro Galvao after just four minutes, although the referee didn’t blow for a foul. Then, just two minutes later, Bebeto tricked Puebla, who brought the Brazilian down and then appeared to stamp on his thigh. This time the referee saw fit to show Puebla a yellow card to calm the Chilean down.

Recent findings suggest that the game continued with Brazil enjoying most of the possession but Chile remaining disciplined in defence. Although it was Chile who needed the win, they seemed focused on trying to reach half-time without conceding, rather than attempting to score. Brazil were creating chances, especially through Careca, but goalkeeper Roberto Rojas was equal to everything. Whenever Chile did venture into the Brazilian half, they were usually swiftly dispossessed.

Recent findings suggest that with Chile sitting deep, most of Brazil’s efforts were from distance – they were having difficulty penetrating the tight defence. Just before half-time, Branco hit a hard, swerving shot that Rojas did well to adjust to and save. And with that, the teams went into the break still scoreless.

It has been revealed that brazil started the second half where they had left off previously – on the attack. And finally, four minutes in, they broke the deadlock. A defensive header from Branco fell to Dunga who played a quick ball forward to Bebeto. Spinning towards goal, he cleared one challenge before hitting a through ball to Careca. The Napoli star sidestepped Puebla before hitting a shot that, although partially saved by Rojas, went in. Brazil were 1-0 up and heading for Italia 90. Chile were facing elimination.

For the following five minutes, Chile dominated as they tried desperately to get back into the tie. Brazil weathered the storm before taking control once again. It was impossible to see where Chile would get two goals from, which would mean committing men forward, leaving gaps for Bebeto and Careca to exploit. Then came the dramatic moment of the game.

In a recent development, on 68 minutes, Chile had possession of the ball in their own half through Astengo when a huge roar suddenly burst out from the crowd. TV cameras swivelled across to goalkeeper Rojas who lay in his penalty area while something flamed and smoked beside him. As the cameras lingered, it appeared as though a flare had been thrown by someone, Chilean players rushing to Rojas’ aid. As they understood what had happened, tempers began to rise. Patricio Yanez made several obscene gestures at the Brazilian fans.

The Chileans motioned for a stretcher but, with none immediately forthcoming, took the initiative and carried their stricken goalkeeper off the field. The cameras demonstrated blood running down the back of Rojas’ head as he was carried down the stairs into the tunnel, along with his teammates.

The stunned Brazilian players discussed what to do next with the referee, spending a further 20 minutes on the pitch awaiting the return of the Chileans. Eventually, the referee was forced to abandon the game, meaning that the likely solution would be a replay at a neutral venue. It appeared that Brazil had been just 22 minutes from Italy before their unruly fans ruined the day.

Industry observers note that as mentioned, the TV cameras had swivelled to Rojas after the crowd noise drew attention to the incident. There was no footage of Rojas being hit by the flare, just his injured body writhing in agony on the floor. But one pitchside photographer, Paulo Teixeira, had seen the flare come onto the field – and something struck him as not quite right.

Sources indicate that he could see Rojas bleeding from near his eye but was sure that the flare had landed many feet away from him. In a CNN interview, he recalled his immediate reaction: “I missed the shot and so did most of the photographers. But there was one guy by me, Ricardo Alfieri, a good friend, and I asked him, ‘Ricardo, did you capture the flare?’ He stated, ‘Of course, about 4-5 shots.'”.

In a recent development, alfieri worked for a Japanese publication and so had to send his unprocessed film to them the next morning. Teixeira realised that he needed to move fast if his gut instinct was correct. Finding a local radio reporter, he convinced him to put Alfieri on air, who told listeners that he had shots that indicated the flare had not struck Rojas.

Recent findings suggest that immediately after, the Brazilian football president, Ricardo Teixeira, came to the station and asked about the film. Together, they found a local lab and, dragging a poor technician out on a Sunday night, had her warm the lab up for the next four hours. Finally, they were able to process Alfieri’s film.

In a recent development, teixeira takes up the story again. “When the pictures came out, there were four clear shots – starting with the device flying and then landing one meter away from Rojas. [CBF president] Teixeira was so relieved.”.

The photos were published the next day by local news agency Globo while CBF President Teixeira flew to FIFA’s headquarters in Switzerland. There was clear evidence now that the flare had not directly injured Rojas. But if that was the case, what had caused the bleeding seen on his head?

According to recent reports, two days on from the game, the medical report from the incident stated that there had been no burn marks on Rojas, just a cut on the left side of his forehead. Now back in Santiago, Rojas released a statement saying that he was shocked that people were doubting the nature of his injury.

Rojas’ club side, Sao Paulo, were also publicly expressing doubts about keeping him on the books Finally, five days later, FIFA came to their decision: due to the lack of burn marks and Chile refusing to play on, the game was awarded to Brazil by a 2-0 margin. The Selecao had qualified for yet another World Cup.

Recent findings suggest that but the mystery hadn’t been settled. Had a Brazilian thrown the firecracker? And how did the wound on the forehead arise? The first question was soon solved. It had been thrown by a Brazilian, a 24-year-old woman by the name of Rosenery Mello. After she was named in the press, she became a minor celebrity, leading to a cover pose in the November 1989 Brazilian edition of Playboy and the nickname “Maracana Rocket”.

Industry observers note that the reason for her decision to appear on the cover? The CBF had fined her $12,000 for throwing the flare, while she was allegedly getting $40,000 for the cover.

So now we knew where the flare came from that missed Rojas, but we still didn’t know what had caused the wound. The answer finally came out when Rojas was questioned further in the ensuing days.

He had concealed a razor blade in his glove ahead of the match in order to simulate injury should the need arise. Just think about that for a minute – a professional player had decided before a vital World Cup qualifier to have a blade ready with which to cut himself should he feel it was necessary.

Incredibly, this wasn’t something Rojas had cooked up himself; both manager Orlando Aravena and team doctor Daniel Rodriguez were also involved. The whole scheme had, in fact, been concocted in the training camp to get the game abandoned at any sign of crowd trouble or player fighting.

Recent findings suggest that unsurprisingly, Rojas was given a lifetime ban from the game, which was finally rescinded in 2001, allowing him to return to Sao Paulo as a goalkeeping coach and then manager. Chile were also barred from the 1994 World Cup qualification process, although more because of abandoning the game than the injury simulation.

In a recent development, both Aravena and Rodriguez, along with the president of the Chilean football federation, Sergio Stoppel, and the captain, Fernando Astengo, were punished by FIFA. Astengo has protested his innocence to this day, swearing he had no knowledge of the plan.

According to recent reports, this is not the only example over the years of what might be termed an “overreaction” to objects thrown from the crowd during a game. Of course, any such action by fans is deplorable and it is only natural that they should suffer sanctions But that has not prevented such actions sometimes being milked by the victims. The two best-known examples are probably the infamous Borussia Monchengladbach Coke can and the Celtic bottle.

Recent findings suggest that the Coke can incident occurred during the 1971/72 European Cup when Borussia Monchengladbach hosted Inter. With the Germans leading 2-1, Inter legend Roberto Boninsegna seemed to be hit on the head by an object, suddenly falling to the ground.

The object turned out to be a Coke can. Gladbach’s Gunter Netzer had his wits about him and disposed of the offending item, before Sandro Mazzola grabbed another from a fan and presented it to the referee. The upshot was that Gladbach won 7-1, but Inter managed to persuade UEFA to annul the game and replay it. Inter ended up proceeding to the final against Ajax.

The second incident occurred when Celtic hosted Rapid Wien in the 1984/85 Cup Winners’ Cup. In a game that was already boiling over as Celtic took a 3-0 lead saw a penalty awarded to the Bhoys. As the Austrian players argued with the referee, a bottle was thrown onto the pitch from the Celtic crowd.

Sources indicate that like the Brazilian flare, it missed everyone, but that didn’t stop Rapid’s Rudi Weinhofer from collapsing, holding his face before being taken off, his head heavily bandaged by the physio. Like Gladbach, Celtic were ordered to replay the game at a neutral venue – Old Trafford – and also were eliminated.

In a recent development, but both incidents were just feigning injury; they were not quite at the scale of concealing and then cutting yourself with a razor. And the truth is that, had it not been due to the quick thinking of a Brazilian photojournalist, Chile may have succeeded. Nowadays, such a rouse would be impossible given all the camera angles and mobile phone footage. But back then, it was a different ballgame.

To paraphrase the Scooby Doo series, “Chile would have gotten away with it if it wasn’t for those meddling photographers.” It is a funny old game, indeed.

Né à Firminy, conseiller municipal de Saint-Etienne (depuis 8 mois) et parlementaire le plus investi dans le soutien aux ultras stéphanois (il avait été un des premiers signataires de notre pétition lancée le printemps 2025 et ayant recueilli plus de 5 800 signatures), le député PS ligérien Pierrick Courbon (41 ans) a posté cet après-midi le message suivant sur son compte Instagram.

Recent findings suggest that "Ce qui s'est passé à Reims est inacceptable ! Les supporters ne sont pas des sous-citoyens, encore moins du bétail. Je saisis le Ministre de l'Intérieur. Malgré trois décisions de justice confirmant l'absence d'interdiction d'accès au stade tout comme les déplacements en autocars, les supporters stéphanois ont été interpellés à proximité du stade Auguste-Delaune, et contraints de faire demi-tour sous escorte policière. Il est indéniable que des erreurs ont été commises par les services de l'Etat, et qu'un contournement des décisions de justice a eu lieu.

Industry observers note that les supporters ne sont pas des sous-citoyens. Pourtant, depuis de nombreuses années, le supportérisme est un laboratoire commode de mesures sécuritaires et liberticides, qui ne seraient toélérées dans un autre pan de la société. Comme je m'y suis engagé dès samedi, je viens d'alerter Laurent Nunez pour demander des réponses et des explications. La gestion des supporters en France est catastrophique. Je continuerai de les défendre car l'enjeu dépasse le simple cadre sportif.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

von Next Generation am 20.10.2026 in den Kategorien Uncategorized mit 0 Kommentaren.

Sources indicate that A 6-1 reads like a game in which everything fell apart. Look at how the goals came about one by one and a different picture emerges: it was not six separate problems but two or three, which Bayern punished in seven variations. No pressure on the man in possession, marking problems in central areas, and a back line that did not work with the movements in front of it – that chain runs through practically every goal conceded.

This aspect analysis therefore takes the goals rather than the game as its material and works back from there to the patterns.

According to recent reports, bayern triggered very high throughout, stayed tight to their opponents and pushed through centrally without hesitation. Vandevoordt was pressed from Bayern’s right, with the clear intention of keeping him away from the left-hand build-up route and forcing the long ball. Leipzig’s front line of Nusa and Brajan Gruda repeatedly angled their runs deep against Nathaniel Brown and Konrad Laimer.

Industry observers note that bayern had one extra central player dropping into midfield in this phase, usually Kimmich. Had Leipzig played short to the right, he could have pressed through onto Raum; in practice he stayed central and pushed through from there. That left Leipzig with the long ball, and it was ineffective: it produced almost no regains, so the enforced forward play brought neither relief nor territory.

Sources indicate that going the other way, Leipzig got no access at all, and the reason was Bayern’s rotations. Kimmich dropped right, Pavlović left into a back three, with Upamecano holding a very wide position. Against this shifting three-man build-up Leipzig never found a trigger, because the assignments reset with every rotation – whoever was supposed to step out of midfield first had to work out who he was picking up. The handover of pressing duties out of central areas failed repeatedly.

In front of that, Bayern staggered their shape so that Leipzig’s compactness became the problem. Olise moved into the ten space at times, Nathaniel Brown operated in the half-lane and ran beyond from there, Luis Díaz stayed wide left. Saibari and Kane pinned several opponents centrally while regularly pulling out of the central lane. Because Leipzig pressed very narrow, this produced exactly what Bayern were looking for: once the opponent was committed near the ball, the switch followed, and on the now open side stood a one-on-one.

Sources indicate that that already builds the bridge to the goals. The isolated one-on-ones in which Luis Díaz got his three finishes were not individual moments but the product of this sequence of pinning and switching.

Sources indicate that 1-0, Luis Díaz (12.) – The first goal already contains the full diagnosis. Kimmich receives centrally without any pressure and can turn out with an open body shape. Ahead of him Saibari and Kane occupy the central zone in front of the box, which forces Orban and Lukeba to step out – so far, the intended part. The full-backs, however, do not push up with that movement and stay too deep, while Raum’s position plays the runner onside. Klostermann stays outside and leaves the inside lane unsecured, and that is exactly where Luis Díaz starts from. Out of that unprotected lane Díaz runs into the back line and Kimmich chips the ball in behind. Not one bad decision, but four players whose decisions did not fit together.

In a recent development, 2-0, Aleksandar Pavlović (26.) – Same cause, different route. Kane drops deep and Leipzig do not shift across as a unit – the reactions showed it clearly: arms thrown up, gesturing, hands dropping again, the beginnings of frustration. Kane gets the free body shape, and with him the consequence is predictable: the long ball, high or flat. Because Leipzig are so narrow centrally, the ball flies straight through the entire zone in front of their back line. Luis Díaz moves actively into the passing lane to control it while Klostermann tries to get into his running line and does not make it – Díaz reaches the ball first. From the one-on-one he wins, Díaz dribbles centrally at Orban, which creates a four-against-three on the break. Díaz pins Orban and Lukeba centrally, Pavlović overlaps on the left after holding a high, left-leaning position all evening and threatening the back line. Two touches, left foot, finished away from the defender.

In a recent development, 3-0, Michael Olise (34.) – Here Bayern’s press shows itself at its clearest. From a Leipzig throw-in, the man-orientation is fully visible: consistent pushing through, clean handovers. A misplaced pass from Raum then cannot be defended, because neither the tracking nor the duelling is good enough to disturb the pass. Kane can open up half-way. Centrally, Olise comes inside from the wing, and Banzuzi and his partner fail to pick him up, letting him run through – against a player of that variability, an invitation to the key pass. Luis Díaz runs beyond and drags Orban with him, Klostermann is pinned wide by Saibari and can no longer get back into central areas. Olise finishes against the goalkeeper’s movement, across his standing leg into the far corner, catching Vandevoordt completely on the wrong foot.

4-0, Luis Díaz (47.) – After a regain, Bayern switch quickly to the far side and once diagonally through, putting Díaz in a one-on-one again. He holds the ball in the dribble, and Leipzig fail to solve the situation in three steps: the centre is not closed, Orban is too late stepping out, Klostermann does not get into the duel. That Vandevoordt leaves the far corner open is the final piece of an isolated one-on-one that should never have arisen.

5-0, Harry Kane (53.) – Structurally the most interesting goal. Leipzig play a long ball without preparing it and react to the consequences contradictorily: the back line does not push up at all, while the midfield line and both forwards counterpress forwards. The ten space opens up enormously, the gaps between the lines become huge – and Olise is standing in that zone. One pass from Kim is enough to take six Leipzig players out of the game. Olise runs unopposed at the back line and lays it off to Díaz, who is in a one-on-one again; Brown joins for the two-against-one and shifts into the inside lane. Klostermann does not pick up his run from the deep half-space, and centrally Kane again drops into Orban’s blind side – a pattern that stood out across the whole game. The result is a two-against-one against the goalkeeper.

6-0, Luis Díaz (69.) – From a set piece Bayern create a five-against-four out wide. Gnabry pins opponents and makes the space for Díaz, Orban again takes one big step in the block and does not get into the duel. The same scene as the 4-0, only from a different phase of play – a sign that this is a behavioural pattern rather than a snapshot.

It has been revealed that 6-1, Andrija Maksimović (90.+1) – Leipzig’s goal indicates in reverse what their own game had been missing. Bayern drop into a deeper block here, and Leipzig combine centrally before going wide. Gruda gets into a one-on-one against Brown, Upamecano steps across – but from above, with too wide a gap and without closing the centre. That opens the one-two, which Leipzig take immediately. Because the whole situation narrows onto that combination, the space behind it stays unoccupied, and Maksimović can take two touches on his left and finish unopposed.

The sequence of goals reads like a repetition. Five of Bayern’s six come from the same combination of no pressure on the ball centrally and a back line that does not manage the space behind it. Luis Díaz stands in an isolated one-on-one three times, Orban is twice too late with a step that is too big, Kane repeatedly drops into his blind side. Klostermann certainly did not have his best day – but it would be too easy to settle the bill with him. In the decisive scenes he faced situations that functioning protection in front of him should never have allowed to arise in the first place.

It has been revealed that behind it all lies not an individual problem but a structural one: Leipzig pressed narrow and found no trigger against Bayern’s rotating back three. That very compactness made the switch of play the opponent’s most effective tool, and at the end of every switch stood a one-on-one that Leipzig lost. The scoreline is not the story – the story is that the same scene worked six times.

Secondo quanto riportato da Corriere dello Sport, Gattuso ha parlato nelle ultime settimane con diversi giocatori per conoscerne gli umori e, finora, ha raccolto soltanto segnali favorevoli alla permanenza. Nel parlare di famiglia ha richiamato anche il «senso di appartenenza» dei giocatori. È su questo legame che punta per trattenere i protagonisti della squadra, mentre cominciano a circolare le prime voci di mercato.

Gattuso ha cercato di coinvolgere tutti, dando spazio anche a chi in precedenza si sentiva fuori posto. In a recent development, da giorni circolano interessamenti per gli olandesi Taylor e Noslin e per i danesi Isaksen e Provstgaard. Isaksen è stato tra i primi a esprimersi pubblicamente sul proprio futuro. Il Brentford di Matthew Benham lo corteggia: l’imprenditore britannico è noto per il lavoro svolto con Brentford e Midtjylland, il club nel quale l’esterno danese è emerso. Benham conosce bene il calcio danese.

Industry observers note that alla prospettiva della Premier League, Isaksen ha risposto: «La Premier? Voglio la Champions con la Lazio». Anche Provstgaard piace da tempo in Inghilterra. Remembering the disaster of 1991/92, Bayern Munich’s worst season in modern history

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mention the words ‘Bayern Munich’ and what comes to mind?
  • It has been revealed that it is a team that has won the European Cup six times and includes such notable alumni as Franz Beckenbauer, Gerd Muller, Sepp Maier, Karl-Heinz Rummenigge, Lothar Matthaus and Philipp Lahm.
  • But hard as it is to believe, they have endured ups and downs just like all teams – the difference being that a Bayern “down” is still normally what most other teams dream about.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mention the words ‘Bayern Munich’ and what comes to mind? A teutonic powerhouse? One of Europe’s elite? Serial winners? The Bavarians are, after all, a team that has won the Bundesliga 31 times – when the first was only 55 years ago.

It has been revealed that it is a team that has won the European Cup six times and includes such notable alumni as Franz Beckenbauer, Gerd Muller, Sepp Maier, Karl-Heinz Rummenigge, Lothar Matthaus and Philipp Lahm. It is a world-famous brand that stands for excellence. Bayern Munich equals trophies and success.

But hard as it is to believe, they have endured ups and downs just like all teams – the difference being that a Bayern “down” is still normally what most other teams dream about.

But there is one season that will always live in infamy in Bayern history, a season during the 1990s when they were, frankly speaking, pretty terrible. Of course, terrible for Die Roten is relative – we are not talking about relegation here – but by their lofty standards, they turned into a mediocre team for 12 months. The season in question took place across 1991/92.

What’s more surprising is that there was no immediate sign beforehand of the slump to come. The 1986/87 campaign had seen an Udo Lattek-led Bayern win the Bundesliga, the manager whom Die Roten had dominated Europe under in the 1970s.

That proved to be his final season before being replaced by Jupp Heynckes, who ironically had also replaced Lattek when he became Borussia Monchengladbach manager in 1979. While unable to replicate the Foals’ amazing 1970s success, Heynckes did lead them to fourth-place finishes in 1985 and 1986, followed by third place in 1987 along with a UEFA Cup semi-final, putting him on Bayern’s radar.

Sources indicate that heynckes’ debut season (1987/88) saw Bayern fail to retain their title as an emergent Werder Bremen secured glory under the stewardship of Otto Rehhagel. With strikers Karl-Heinz Riedle and Frank Neubarth, and a defence that conceded just 22 goals in 34 games, Bremen finished four points ahead of second-place Bayern, having beaten them 3-1 in a key week 26 meeting. But normal service was soon resumed as Bayern lifted the Bundesliga the following year while also reaching the semi-finals of the UEFA Cup.

Industry observers note that the 1989/90 season saw Bayern even more dominant, again winning the Bundesliga by six points while this time reaching the semi-finals of the European Cup, before falling to the AC Milan of the three Dutch masters. Looking at the squad that season, it is notable that there were no world-renowned stars. The strike duo of Roland Wohlfarth and Alan McInally, while efficient, were hardly names that would’ve had Baresi, Maldini and co worried. But it was still enough to dominate Germany.

As such, the summer of 1990 saw Heynckes strengthen the squad by bringing in Stefan Effenberg, Brian Laudrup and Christian Ziege. Of these, the signing of Effenberg was by far the most interesting. A player who throughout his career would be no stranger to controversy, he was asked about why he had decided to join Bayern. Sporting his blonde mullet, he replied, “Because the other clubs are too stupid to win the Bundesliga.”.

It was a surefire way to place a target on your back for the season, a comment sure to have been posted on opposing dressing room walls, including Kaiserslautern’s. An early season league game saw Bayern hammer Kaiserslautern 4-0 at the Olympiastadion before the season then developed into a battle between both teams for the title.

Sources indicate that late March saw the advantage swing to Kaiserslautern as they defeated Bayern 2-1 at home courtesy of a late winner from Stefan Kuntz. That sparked a strong run from Die Roten and, with three matches to go, things were tight.

Bayern then travelled to Bochum to face little-fancied Wattenscheid – a team that played in the tiny Lohrheidestadion and who Bayern had beaten 7-0 earlier in the season. To the shock of a watching nation, Wattenscheid held a 2-1 lead as the game entered the dying minutes. Then, with just three minutes left, the ever-reliable Wohlfarth scored to save Bayern’s blushes. Or so it seemed.

Two minutes later, Thorsten Fink scored a shock winner for the team from Bochum to send 35,000 fans delirious – a defeat that opened the door for Kaiserslautern to claim their first Bundesliga title.

It has been revealed that as if the defeat to Wattenscheid wasn’t painful enough, Bayern also suffered heartache in the European Cup. Once again, the semi-final curse raised its head, this time to Eastern European opposition rather than Italian. A strong team had emerged at Red Star Belgrade, who came to Munich and left with a 2-1 win in the first leg of their semi-final clash.

It has been revealed that that left Bayern with a tough assignment in front of 80,000 rabid Red Star fans – flares burning in an intimidating atmosphere. But Die Roten rose to the task and the game was about to enter extra-time with Bayern 2-1 up when a freak own goal from captain Klaus Augenthaler in the last minute saw the Yugoslavs grab the all-important equaliser and move on to the final.

It has been revealed that so as 1991/92 commenced, Bayern came off disappointment at the end of the preceding season but had still finished second in the league and narrowly missed on a European Cup final appearance. It was a season that many teams would die for.

In a recent development, the squad development continued as Heynckes brought in players such as Jan Wouters, Oliver Kreuzer, Thomas Berthold and two Brazilians, Mazinho and Bernardo. But balancing that was the retirement of long-serving stalwart Augenthaler. Still, Bayern fans were looking forward to reclaiming their position at the top of the league while perhaps claiming a UEFA Cup title.

According to recent reports, the opening two league games saw an inauspicious start as Bayern drew at Werder Bremen before losing at home to Bundesliga fresh boys Hansa Rostock. They then travelled to Dusseldorf and came away with their first win, albeit only 1-0 thanks to a last-minute winner from Mazinho. Fans could start to relax ahead of a straightforward cup tie at home against minnows FC Homburg.

Homburg is a small town in the Saarland region of Germany and their local team had been relatively obscure for most of its history. But, in 1986, they had reached the Promised Land of the Bundesliga for the first time. Their fans enjoyed two seasons at the top table before being relegated and then returning immediately. And so, travelling to Munich, the team was a second-tier outfit who typically played in front of 8,000 fans, even when in the Bundesliga.

Only 9,000 bothered to trek to the Olympiastadion to watch the tie, resulting in a strange atmosphere within the vast bowl. It took 27 minutes but Bayern grabbed the lead through a backpost header from Mazinho. So far, so good. But Homburg emerged in the second half revitalised and had the cheek to equalise via a powerful shot from Rodolfo Cardoso.

Industry observers note that worse was to come for Bayern as, with just 13 minutes remaining, a loose ball fell to Homburg’s Matthias Baranowski, who gladly accepted the gift. This was not in the Bayern script and could not be permitted. Unsurprisingly, while Homburg fans were still rubbing their eyes, Mazinho scored again. Enough of this nonsense.

Industry observers note that and so the game went into extra-time when Bayern’s fitness would surely overwhelm the underdogs. But just five minutes in, Homburg’s Michael Kimmel jinked into the area and scored with a low shot. That pesky Homburg side just didn’t know when to lie down. And if that wasn’t bad enough, they then scored again four minutes later through Bernd Gries. Bayern were 4-2 down at home. That was how the game would end. A shocked Bayern had been eliminated in their first cup game by a lower division team in their own stadium.

Sometimes a cup defeat can be a blessing in disguise – at least now they could focus on the league and UEFA Cup. Maybe all was not lost yet.

Their league form continued to fluctuate and, after nine matches, Bayern sat in seventh place as they prepared to commence their continental campaign. A relatively easy first-round draw saw them due to travel to Ireland for a first leg against Cork City. As Bayern fans researched where Cork was on the map, the players flew over.

It has been revealed that cork City had only formed in 1984, following the bankruptcy of Cork United in 1982. A second-place league finish in the previous season had seen the part-timers earn their spot in the UEFA Cup. In front of just 4,000 fans, it was time for Bayern to forget about the Homburg embarrassment and start a successful UEFA Cup campaign.

Sources indicate that dave Barry was a local who enjoyed a successful career with Cork County, playing Gaelic Football and winning two All-Ireland medals. But he also enjoyed regular football on the side and so turned out for Cork City as a midfielder. Ahead of the game, he had somehow come to the attention of Effenberg who, with his normal diplomacy, compared him to his grandfather.

In a recent development, picked for the game against Bayern, he wrote his name into Irish folklore when, after just 26 minutes, Cork stole the ball from the advancing Bayern defence and Barry found it at his feet. Charging forward, the balding midfielder turned inside one defender before rifling a shot home. The fans went ballistic.

In a recent development, and so it stood until just before half-time when Effenberg finally brought parity to the score. Everyone then braced for the second-half whirlwind from Bayern, but it never occurred. The part-timers of Cork ended with a famous 1-1 draw against the German giants.

Recent findings suggest that the second leg saw Bayern struggle once more. In fact, the Irish part-timers held out until the 71st minute before Bruno Labbadia finally spared Bayern’s blushes. A last-gasp penalty added a little more gloss, but at the final whistle, Die Roten had only just got over the line. Considering this and the Homburg result, all was most definitely not well in Bavaria.

Recent findings suggest that three days later, Bayern travelled to Stuttgart and were hammered 4-1 – not by VfB but rather by Stuttgarter Kickers. It was finally too much to bear and, three days later, Bayern announced that they were parting manufacturer with Heynckes.

According to recent reports, the former striking great went on to enjoy a long and successful managerial career, overseeing teams in Spain, Portugal and Germany, including Real Madrid, Benfica, Schalke and his first love, Borussia Monchengladbach. He even returned to Bayern, becoming caretaker manager in 2009 after the firing of Jurgen Klinsmann before replacing Louis van Gaal in 2011 and leading them to a Champions League final defeat to Chelsea.

He then giuded Bayern to glory in 2013 by defeating Bundesliga rivals Borussia Dortmund in the final, making Heynckes just the fourth manager to win the competition with two different teams, Real Madrid being the other. One of the all-time greats, his dismissal after the Kickers defeat was later described by general manager Uli Hoeness as “the biggest mistake I ever made in my business life”.

According to recent reports, A meeting was set up with club legend Franz Beckenbauer in Munich’s Sheraton Hotel to offer him the position as head coach. But he declined, stating prior commitments made it impossible. And therefore Bayern turned elsewhere – with a somewhat surprising result.

Replacing Heynckes at the helm would be Danish legend Soren Lerby. A player who enjoyed three seasons with Bayern, during which they won two Bundesliga titles, he had only recently retired from playing at the age of 32. Taking the Bayern job represented his first step into management – a daunting task for experienced heads let alone a rookie. He didn’t even have the required coaching licence at the time of his appointment. It seemed a strange choice to most fans.

His tenure started off shakily as Bayern lost successive league games against Dortmund and VfB Stuttgart to drop to 14th in the 20-team league, just three places above the relegation spots. Next up for Lerby was, ironically, a trip back to Denmark as Bayern had drawn Boldklubben 1903 in the second round of the UEFA Cup. If Lerby thought it would be an enjoyable trip home, he was in for a major surprise.

Not even the most hardcore Boldklubben fans can claim that their team had a grand history. They had won the league seven times, but four of those were before World War Two, while the most recent was back in 1976, before then merging with Kjobenhavns Boldklub in 1992 to form FC Copenhagen, who have enjoyed considerable success since.

It has been revealed that they had only ever won two European ties and never made it past the second round. The visit of Bayern would represent one of the last games that Boldklubben would play before the merger. And what a game it was.

According to recent reports, over 14,000 fans packed into the Gentofte Stadion to see how their boys would fare against the German powerhouse. For 30 minutes the game was a stalemate, until Bayern snatched the lead through Mazinho. That lead lasted just five minutes before Michael Manniche tied the game. Tied going into the half-time break, there was little indication of the shockwave to come.

After 57 minutes, Boldklubben earned a penalty, which was duly dispatched by Danish star Ivan Nielsen. Four minutes later, the fans were in ecstasy as Kenneth Wegner made it 3-1. As the ground began to shake, the madness continued; just three minutes later, Manniche grabbed a second to put the Danes 4-1 up. The mighty Bayern had just conceded three goals in the space of seven minutes. And it wasn’t over yet.

It has been revealed that brian Klaus added a fifth before Peter Uldbjerg made it 6-1. No-one could quite believe what they were witnessing. Markus Munch pulled back a last-minute consolation for Bayern but, as the final whistle sounded, all eyes turned to the scoreboard: Boldklubben 1903 6-2 Bayern Munich. Bayern’s season had just truly imploded.

In a recent development, the return leg two weeks later saw Die Roten exit the competition with a whimper, winning just 1-0 through a late Mazinho goal. They had now been eliminated from the DFB-Pokal at home by a lower division side, from the UEFA Cup by Danish minnows and were sitting in 14th place in the league.

Given this start, it was no real surprise that Lerby was a dead man walking. He managed to stumble on until March when a 4-0 defeat away at Kaiserslautern saw Bayern, still stuck in the lower half of the table, finally wield the axe. It was to represent Lerby’s only stint in football management.

It was time for a third manager that season as Hoeness turned to a much more experienced hire in Erich Ribbeck.

Ribbeck had started his managerial career back in 1967 at Rot-Weiss Essen before managing Eintracht Frankfurt, Kaiserslautern, Borussia Dortmund and Bayer Leverkusen. His stats to date were at best mediocre – the only trophy he won during that period was the UEFA Cup with Bayer Leverkusen in 1988 – but he had Bundesliga experience and so was seen as the man who could right the listing ship.

But Bayern by now were in a complete funk and so Ribbeck oversaw a final 11 league games in which they won five but lost as many as they stumbled over the finishing line, mired in mediocrity.

With the season over, Bayern sat in tenth, exactly mid-table. They had lost more games than they had won, including seven at home, and finished with a -2 goal difference. As usual, Wohlfarth was top scorer with 17, followed by Mazinho (12) and Effenberg (11). They had to sit back and watch while VfB Stuttgart, Dortmund and Frankfurt played out final-day drama to captivate the whole country.

It has been revealed that all three teams sat on 50 points going into the final matchday and all three were playing away from home. Frankfurt had goal difference advantage and just needed to win, but shockingly lost to Hansa Rostock while having a clear penalty denied to them at 1-1.

Dortmund won at Duisburg and were two minutes from being Bundesliga champions before Guido Buchwald wrote himself into Stuttgart legend with an 88th-minute winner at Leverkusen – despite being down to ten men following the sending-off of Matthias Sammer – earning Stuttgart the title on goal difference.

That summer saw Bayern spend significant. In came Thomas Helmer, Jorginho, Mehmet Scholl and, most newsworthy, the return of the prodigal son, Lothar Matthaus. Laudrup and Effenberg were moved on to Fiorentina to help fund the rebuild.

Sources indicate that it worked: Bayern finished second in the Bundesliga, just a point behind champions Werder Bremen and with just five losses and a +29 goal difference. Ribbeck had successfully steadied the ship and would soon retire, replaced by Beckenbauer before a disastrous spell as Germany manager from 1998 to 2000. But Ribbeck also left with the unenviable stat of becoming the first and only manager of Bayern to be in charge for over 500 days without winning a single trophy.

According to recent reports, to this day, the 1991/92 season stands as a nadir for Bayern. Since the, Die Roten have only ever finished outside the top three twice, and have won 12 Bundesliga titles and three Champions Leagues. While 90s was often an inconsistent decade for Bayern – with players more often featured in the gossip pages rather than the sports pages, leading to the famous “FC Hollywood” nickname – nothing was as bad as 1991/92.

It has been revealed that bayern will always represent one of the elite European teams and are the gold standard against which many others measure themselves. Moreover, they have enjoyed success without the huge external financial backing that some other European sides have enjoyed.

It has been argued by many that their recent dominance of German football has spoilt the Bundesliga as a spectacle, especially considering their ten successive. But it is refreshing to know that even teams like Bayern Munich can experience a season of woe. For that one year, they were actually human after all. And for that, VfB Stuttgart, Homborg, Cork City and Boldklubben will be eternally grateful.

Les U15 avec brio chez les Sanpriods

  • Les U15 de Benjamin Petit, après leur précieuse victoire d'il y a deux semaines contre Villefranche (1-0) se déplaçaient cet après-midi sur le terrain de l'AS Saint-Priest, qui n'est jamais un adversaire facile.

  • La composition : Clapeyron - Bergougnoux, Wojcik, Bastide, Uneau - Boukerma, Lebreton (L.La Rosa, 45ème), M.La Rosa (Linganzi Koumba, 40ème) - Fernandes (Moutae, 50ème), Bangoura, Davignon.

Les U15 de Benjamin Petit, après leur précieuse victoire d'il y a deux semaines contre Villefranche (1-0) se déplaçaient cet après-midi sur le terrain de l'AS Saint-Priest, qui n'est jamais un adversaire facile. Auparavant, dans la semaine, mercredi, à Cruas, ils s'étaient mesurés à l'Olympique de Marseille, leader de la poule Méditerranée, et qui, en match amical, a largement battu bon nombre d'équipes de renom. Les jeunes Verts avaient mieux fait que se défendre, ne s'inclinant que sur le score de 2 à 1. Revenons-en au match d'aujourd'hui pour dire que la victoire est revenue en toute logique aux jeunes Verts sur le score de 2 à 1, une victoire qui va leur permettre d'engranger des points et....de la confiance.

Ce sont les Sanpriods qui ont ouvert la marque, contre le cours du jeu, à la 19ème minute sur une approximation défensive. Mais les Verts réagissaient immédiatement et, deux minutes plus tard, à la 21ème, Kaïs Boukerma, sur une passe de Charly Davignon, de l'entrée de la surface, plaçait une frappe au ras du poteau pour l'égalisation. Un quart d'heure plus tard, à la 36ème, Hugo Bastide, qui opérait aujourd'hui en défense centrale, récupérait fort à propos un 2ème ballon sur un corner pour donner l'avantage aux Verts. Ce fut difficile après le repos, car Saint-Priest mettait la pression pour revenir au score. Mais les Verts faisaient preuve de solidarité et de rigueur défensive pour conserver cet avantage de 2 à 1.A noter la victoire des U14 sur le score de 8 à 1. Nous reviendrons ultérieurement sur la belle saison de cette équipe.

La composition : Clapeyron - Bergougnoux, Wojcik, Bastide, Uneau - Boukerma, Lebreton (L.La Rosa, 45ème), M.La Rosa (Linganzi Koumba, 40ème) - Fernandes (Moutae, 50ème), Bangoura, Davignon.

La réaction de Benjamin Petit : "Nous avons fait une bonne première mi-temps, même si nous avons un peu manqué de tranchant dans le domaine offensif. Il n'a pas manqué grand chose sur plusieurs situations intéressantes. C'est là un axe de progrès bien identifié que d'aller chercher cette réussite offensive. J'ai apprécié le fait que les garçons soient restés sereins après l'ouverture du score par Saint-Priest. Cela leur a permis de revenir rapidement et de passer devant avant la pause. Par contre, la deuxième mi-temps a été plus compliquée. Saint-Priest nous a mis la pression et nous avons eu plus de mal à construire et à progresser à l'intérieur du jeu. Mais nous avons fait preuve de caractère, de rigueur défensive et cela nous a permis de conserver le résultat.".

Breaking: Access, Not Chances: How Como Took Manchester United Apart – LC

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

von Next Generation am 24.10.2026 in den Kategorien Champions League,Uncategorized mit 0 Kommentaren.

Como beat Manchester United 4-1 — and in this case the scoreline really is a fair expression of the game. For long stretches the match was one-sided, not in terms of chance volume but in terms of access: Como dictated in every phase where the ball went, who received it, and under what conditions it had to be played on. United never got on terms in any of those phases.

Cesc Fàbregas’s side indicated two things that rarely go together. Out of possession, a pressing structure with clear direction, isolation of one side, and man-marking that applied near the ball only for the action in progress while everything around it was already speculating on the second ball. And in possession, a positional game of remarkable technical maturity that ties opponents in, switches play, and works systematically into the space behind them. The 4-1 is therefore less an outlier than evidence of work that has been built up over recent seasons.

This analysis goes through the phases one by one: first Como in possession and United’s response, then the work against the ball from the high press to defending the box, and finally the goals.

In build-up, Como moved away from their nominal 4-2-3-1 and sat closer to a 4-3-3, with the eights as the real variable: very free in their movement and above all active in the half-spaces. The base structure stayed stable — a flat four plus a six in front of them, sometimes ahead of the line, sometimes slightly behind the forward line.

Close to their own goal, Como consistently involved goalkeeper Butez as an additional central player in the build-up. That created a five-against-four against United’s front line — awkward on paper, more awkward still in execution, because Como didn’t use the overload to play through but to tie opponents in. From there, the same shape kept appearing on both the right and the left: centre-back, full-back, a player from the half-position in the eight space, and a six alongside. A diamond that wasn’t an end in itself but had a purpose: the diagonal route out.

Como’s build-up structure. From a 4-1 (flat four), the half-positions with Paz and Perrone are added. Small triangles and diamonds emerge. The three attackers ahead of them create additional options in behind.

One detail deserves particular attention. At times the full-backs stood not wide but flat, in a half-position. That sounds like a nuance, but it had a clear function: it vacated the wing and created the space the eights could drop into — Paz and Perrone did so regularly. If you don’t occupy the wing yourself, you force the opponent to guard it anyway.

ManU got no access near the ball and left large diagonal spaces open on the far side.

Recent findings suggest that for United’s midfielders this was close to unsolvable. Tielemans, Mount and Andrey Santos spent the whole game struggling to establish any responsibility at all, let alone get into duels. When an eight dropped out, they couldn’t follow, and if one of them was tied in by it, a two-against-one opened up on the far wing. Como didn’t create that situation once; they created it serially.

Industry observers note that the decisive mechanism lay in receiving and relaying the ball. The player in the deeper position usually worked with two touches: the first took the ball backwards, the second relayed it to the free teammate. At the end of every one of those actions stood a player with the game in front of him — and from that open position he could switch play.

According to recent reports, what made it possible were the preparatory movements. Paz and captain Da Cunha first lured their markers in the wrong direction and then worked with the head start they’d bought. That head start isn’t only space, it’s above all time: time to control the ball first and relay it second, rather than having to do both in one touch.

A scene in the 17th minute is typical. Mason Mount steps out, Mazraoui goes into the duel at the same time — nominally United are in an overload here. Only neither of them really gets to the opponent, because both are too late. Paz can therefore calmly take his touch backwards and switch play directly with the second, dissolving the pressure before it had even formed.

According to recent reports, when the build-up ran down the right, it demonstrated in a recurring pattern: Paz and Da Cunha took the first touch backwards or inside and then switched with the left foot out of a closed body position. The players they found were systematically in open positions — Milla, the far-side six, or the wing-to-wing connection directly.

Recent findings suggest that in the second half, Como adjusted the shape and more often played with two sixes, to form the diamonds faster and switch to the far-side six faster. Couto stood out in this: the right-back repeatedly played the chip into the six or ten space — six or seven times in a row during one spell. It was mainly Paz who received the ball there and could launch the attack.

In the second half Como focus on those diagonal spaces and look for them mainly with chipped balls.

Especially striking inside the diamond are the rotations between the players. Because of the connections between them, they moved in rotation depending on running path, space and ball movement. The same recurring spaces were re-occupied. Under pressure on the ball carrier, the outer players pushed flat or ran in behind the opponents; the highest player in the diamond burst out of the cover shadow and became the reference point in depth. On a deep pass, the two wide players released and joined the depth, able to offer themselves again immediately in an open body position. If the pass went via the flat wide players, the spaces in front of the fresh ball carrier could be run into. Every rotation, every positional adjustment was coordinated with the others and, in the end, produced a stream of pressure-resolving passes while Manchester United chased the press in vain.

Industry observers note that como bridged the middle third exceptionally quickly, via dribbles at speed and diagonal passes. Behind it stood a recognisable principle: first tie the opponent to one wing, then get behind them via the diagonal, and in the final third do the same thing again. In sum, that produced the shape of a Z — build-up on the right, transition on the left, finish from the right again.

It has been revealed that in this example Como pin ManU in the press with their short passing. Thanks to the extra attacker on the ball-near side they can play through the pressure and switch.

The connections between wingers and striker carried these attacks and were deliberately kept flexible. The wide players sometimes stayed wide, sometimes came short, sometimes tucked inside. Douvikas accordingly either waited deep in front of the line for the chipped ball or, when space opened up on the wing, received the deeper pass and then ran in behind along the wing as soon as the ball sat on the full-back’s open foot. That flexibility produced the overloads on one side, and the overloads produced the central overload.

Industry observers note that in the final third one element was added that is rare in fast transition teams: patience. Como drew opponents towards them with dribbles and short passes, used back-passes when needed, and then switched in front of the block. Da Cunha, Baturina and Paz were the three who could tie opponents in and then find the diagonal. They created the positions on the diagonal, were available to receive, and used their space to apply pressure. The block was usually tied in with short touches, the switch and the position behind the opponent prepared, and quick finishes sought.

According to recent reports, the intensity in possession shouldn’t be underestimated. Practically every attack involved at least three or four players, the width was occupied, the centre likewise, and there were multiple options throughout. What they looked for almost every time was the space behind the opponent on the far side — exactly the zone that is closed last when a block shifts across.

It has been revealed that paz brought the right profile for this pattern. A strong left foot cutting inside from the right, he repeatedly dropped into the right-hand blind side of his opponents, got shots away there with few touches, and racked up the most shots of the match. That the finishes generally came off few touches isn’t a detail but the consequence of the time won further back.

According to recent reports, as the move continues, Como again look for the blind side of the defenders. Here Douvikas and Paz are positioned in behind, with Da Cunha joining in front of the back line. After briefly pinning the opponents, the switch reaches Da Cunha, who misses the target from distance.

According to recent reports, what carries all of this is the technical execution. Soft passes, sharp ones when the moment called for it, consistently well timed and played into the right foot — for ninety minutes. Passing that secure at that tempo is what makes a variable concept actually retrievable.

United’s basic problem out of possession was the hybrid. They pressed half man-oriented, but with a plus-one in the last line — a construction that forces compromises in both directions. It demands access up front that it doesn’t fund at the back.

There were certainly moments when it worked. When Dalot pushed through into the press on the right and passed his man backwards, a clean man-orientation emerged all the way up to the front — and with it a clear assignment for Mount, out of which the ball could be won. But that stayed the exception. Most of the time Dalot sat too flat out of possession, so United couldn’t trigger the duels up front and went into the press a man short.

Mount was the most conspicuous case in this respect. He barely got into a duel across the whole match because the decision to step out always came too late. Against a team that works with preparatory movements, a late decision is practically the same as none: the opponent already has the head start before the journey even begins.

Industry observers note that on top of that came a problem on the far side. There, United’s winger frequently failed to protect the depth — usually Mbeumo, who jogged back rather than closing the space. But that was precisely the target zone of Como’s diagonal switches. It allowed them to change sides almost at will and regularly find an open structure on the other side.

Recent findings suggest that the second half brought no improvement. The distances to opponents stayed large, and centrally what was actually intended still didn’t materialise. Michael Carrick’s double change at half-time was meant to bring more physicality to the six with Carlos Baleba, but it didn’t solve the problem — the assignments still didn’t work, the duels in the centre still didn’t happen, and the wide positions dragged the eights out further, which opened new spaces.

In the end the energy simply wasn’t there to press with the necessary intensity. United’s press became increasingly static, and a static press against an opponent with this passing quality yields not a single ball win — it only hands them the starting positions they’re looking for anyway.

Sources indicate that como started the game in a high press and sustained it above all in the first half, with isolated spells after the break too. It was triggered on back-passes and goal kicks — and, remarkably, by their own goals: after every strike the team immediately pushed high again instead of managing the lead in a deeper block.

Recent findings suggest that the steering ran consistently towards United’s left build-up side. The reason is personnel: Harry Maguire played there with his weaker left foot as the outside foot, and next to him stood another right-footer in Noussair Mazraoui on the left. Two right-footers on one build-up side means the ball always has to be taken back inside to play on — exactly where Como were closing the door. The press was usually triggered by the left-sided forward, with the ball ending up at either Maguire or Mazraoui.

Pressing structure after the change in the second half.

In the centre Como defended man-oriented, with both sixes pushing very high and taking flat passes into United’s midfielders out of the game. That removed the short route through the middle as an option and left the long ball. But the long ball triggered nothing for United: the second balls went to Como practically every time.

That isn’t chance, it’s running work. The sixes consistently tracked the negative pressing paths back, anticipated the long ball early, and were in front of the line before it arrived. Luis Milla covered the most ground of any player on the pitch in this pattern — recovery runs after being played past, doubling up on the ball, attacking the second ball. When the long ball came from Maguire or one of the full-backs, a six was regularly in front of the line with an intense sprint, sealing the centre, taking away the diagonal follow-up passes and attacking the loose balls.

Defending the long ball and extra support on the second ball.

Once the ball was on one side, that side was isolated. The near-side forward had access to the centre-back and dropped back a touch when the pass went to the full-back, so that he covered centre-back and six simultaneously and closed the square pass. The far-side forward marked the goalkeeper. That served two functions at once: it took away United’s escape route via the keeper along with the switch, and it kept a player in position for the moment of the turnover.

Industry observers note that the double pivot worked in a deliberate half-position. The near-side six stayed tight to his man, the far-side one dropped slightly behind him — securing the space and at the same time establishing access to the far-side centre-back in United’s back three.

The last line defended largely man-for-man in the high press, and very tightly. But the decisive detail is the one that carries the whole concept: the man-marking near the ball applied only to the action in progress. Around it, players were already releasing from their assignments and orienting towards the second ball. That is only retrievable at very high intensity — and it’s the reason United’s forced long balls produced not a single usable moment.

Recent findings suggest that when Como dropped a line, the man-orientation at the second height stayed exceptionally high. Here too the back-pass served as the trigger to push up as a unit and tip back into man-marking. If United were in a closed body position, the Comaschi had already pushed up far enough to attack the back-pass at the moment it was played — a pattern that led directly to the 3-0. The half-position was at work there again: closing down level with the centre-back while simultaneously prepared to push through onto the next player deeper.

It has been revealed that in the first half Como still had problems assigning the half-positions against ManU’s 3-2-5. In this example Fernandes moves to the wing, Como fail to establish responsibility and access and are played through at mid-height.

Up to half-time, though, Como had a structural problem with this. The pure man-marking didn’t come off cleanly, because of the two sixes in front of the line, one should really have tucked in and taken over the half-position for the centre-backs. That didn’t happen consistently. The consequence: a centre-back stepped out, the space behind him stayed unoccupied, and that was exactly what United kept attacking.

The pattern of pressing onto Manchester United’s left side continued in the second half, now with Dalot at full-back. The press was still triggered by Douvikas, with the ball-near winger pushing up as a second striker to press the centre-back. Paz focused on the visitors’ ball-near six and Couto pushed through onto Dalot. Through the central connections the game was isolated on one side.

According to recent reports, at half-time Como adjusted. One six moved directly into the line, with the far-side winger pushing in onto the six — they now pressed out of a 5-2-1-2. Lucas Da Cunha pressed through from the right onto Maguire, while Nico Paz picked up United’s six. The central forward pressed the central centre-back and from there carried on to the goalkeeper. The far-side wide midfielder and the remaining six were poised — one onto United’s free six, one onto the far-side centre-back — again in that half-position between opponent and the space to be protected.

ManU building up high against the man-oriented Italians.

Sources indicate that the effect was immediately visible. Como controlled the half-positions, got access right into the last line throughout, and set the rhythm of the match from then on. The adjustment solved exactly the problem the first half had left open, without changing the underlying principle.

Recent findings suggest that in the final phase Como defended from a very deep line inside the box. That left barely any space behind the line to play into — which United hardly looked for anyway. The visitors attacked little depth and rarely occupied the width in the final third, so Como could stay compact without being punished for it.

Accordingly, a lot of players stood very centrally in and in front of the box. That produced numerous cover shadows and a numerical superiority around the ball, which allowed them to steer actively within the block rather than merely react. At times they deliberately steered inside, to guide the opponent into the prepared congestion and cover from a deeper position.

Deep back line in the box, centre closed and play steered inside. The box defending allowed the English side shots from distance.

Sources indicate that the crucial point is that Como left the gaps open not despite this set-up but because of it. If you pack the box and secure the depth, you give up the space in front of the line — and that is exactly where United were supposed to shoot from.

The numbers vindicate the decision. Taking the conceded goal out of the box, Como allowed nine shots from outside the penalty area across ninety minutes, worth roughly 0.24 xG combined; only three of them were even on target. On top of that, of the four shots inside the box, two came from at least 14 to 15 metres and effectively belong in the long-range category as well. United accepted the invitation, and the shooting quality was perfectly decent — it’s just that with that scoring probability over a whole match, the most likely outcome is precisely what happened.

Tracking the ball for the first goal.

1-0, Nico Paz (2′) — The goal comes before United are even set. Como take the goal kick quickly and play straight to the full-back, luring the visitors into the press — only not cleanly. Mason Mount triggers the pressure and is played past, and on the second ball he goes into the duel as well instead of holding the middle and looking for the space where he could pick the ball up. That is exactly what opens the centre, the space for the second ball is there, and Paz can play it through.

Sources indicate that what follows is the transition principle in its purest form: a quick switch to the diagonal side, then short passes against a very deep line. Matheus Cunha doesn’t pick up the player behind him and leaves the ten space open, where Paz is standing. He needs two touches because neither Cunha from above nor Maguire from his distance gets into the duel. Lammens, for his part, doesn’t defend the goal with his cover shadow but takes the near post — which leaves the far corner to a strong left foot. The curled finish into it is quality, though.

2-0, Anastasios Douvikas (49′, assist Paz) — Same zone, same cause. Bryan Mbeumo doesn’t choose to shut the centre but closes the centre-back, which creates the space for Da Cunha, who drives forward and plays Martin Baturina in. Centrally, Mount again fails to pick up his man. Out wide, Amad Diallo, introduced at half-time, generates no pressure centrally, so Mazraoui can’t take over the deep wide player in the first place.

In a recent development, the result is Paz behind the opponent, in the ten space, dribbling unopposed at goal. Matthijs de Ligt establishes no reference to Douvikas’s run in behind and slips as well — a one-against-one with the goalkeeper that Douvikas finishes coolly.

According to recent reports, 3-0, Nico Paz (57′) — The only goal that comes directly out of the work against the ball. Como are in the midfield press in a closed position with access to the inside lane, win the ball there and punish a lapse of concentration in the visitors’ build-up. At the end, Paz is alone in front of Lammens again.

Recent findings suggest that 4-0, Jacobo Ramón (76′, assist Kaiki) — This goal comes from a longer possession spell and highlights the assignment problem in its clearest form. Mazraoui is too narrow and has no access to the wide player. Diallo stands in the space with access to neither the central player nor the full-back nor the winger — an orientation that doesn’t work in any direction.

Recent findings suggest that como switch to Máximo Perrone, who can slide the ball out wide because the space is simply free. From there comes the cross from an open body position, and in the centre Como run a two-against-one at the end of which Ramón scores.

Industry observers note that 4-1, Joshua Zirkzee (90′) — Como’s only lapse, and one in a phase in which the team had already dropped very deep. United get the ball to the wing, it’s two against two in the box, and the cross is initially only feinted. Zirkzee orients himself well forwards at that moment, while Como’s defenders are already stepping out after the feinted cross. Diallo’s ball in behind the line is strong, the offside call is razor-thin in his favour, and Zirkzee takes two touches before finishing one-against-one with the goalkeeper. A blemish, not a structural problem.

The common denominator — Three of Como’s four goals come in the same zone: the space in front of and behind United’s line that nobody takes responsibility for. Mount is involved in two of those scenes through an assignment he never establishes, Diallo in two more after coming on. Nico Paz is at the heart of three of the four goals, twice as scorer, once as the provider — always out of the opponent’s blind side.

Industry observers note that como’s 4-1 has one common cause across every phase, and it lies less in any single idea than in its execution under continuous load. Out of possession they steered, isolated and speculated on the second ball — with man-marking that applied near the ball only for the action in progress and was already dissolved around it. In possession they tied opponents in, switched play and worked systematically into the space behind. Both require eleven players to anticipate a teammate’s decision, and both functioned over the full distance.

Sources indicate that the connecting detail is the half-position. In the press, the far-side six stood between opponent and the space to be protected; in possession, the eights worked out of the same zone, and the full-backs occupied it flat in order to vacate the wing for exactly those players. Como, in other words, occupied the position in both directions from which two jobs can be done at once — which is why the side could neither be played past in the press nor be pinned in the build-up.

For United the diagnosis is more uncomfortable than the result. The problem wasn’t individual errors but that the team never, in any phase, got into the duels it needed. The mixture of half man-orientation and a plus-one in the last line funded no access up front, and without access every decision is made too late — from Mount in the centre to Mbeumo failing to secure the far-side depth. Carrick’s double change at half-time was meant to bring physicality to the six with Carlos Baleba, but it changed nothing about the assignments, and in Diallo a player came on wide who reached neither one opponent nor the other in his space. That the energy ran out in the end was a consequence rather than a cause.

Sources indicate that that leaves the context. A 4-1 against Manchester United is no proof in itself, and Como’s finishing was exceptionally efficient on the night. What showed regardless of the result, though, is a team with a recognisable, rehearsed answer in all four phases of the game — and one that put a technical maturity on the pitch in possession that you wouldn’t readily credit to a side promoted two years ago.

Is attack going to be Manchester United’s best form of defence this season?

There was plenty to like going forward, particularly once United had nudged their way in front after their second lucky break of what had hitherto looked like being a tricky afternoon.

Give this team a little space and they have the attacking players to inflict some serious damage, none more so than Bruno Fernandes who, just five days after collecting the PFA Players’ Player of the Year award, scored a hat-trick in what was another inspired performance.

Ipswich Town will testify to that after a sobering second half when it felt like United were going to score with every raid forward and, for a time, even threaten to equal the nine goals they scored against the promoted side at this ground 31 years ago.

In the returning Marcus Rashford, whom manager Michael Carrick likened to a “newly introduced signing”, Matheus Cunha, Bryan Mbeumo and, of course, Fernandes, United have an intriguing blend of attacking players. Throw in Kobbie Mainoo who, on another day, would have stolen the headlines with an imperious display in central midfield, and one thing United are not lacking for is creativity.

Recent findings suggest that their offensive problems tend to come when opponents sit in and ask to be broken down. Hull City, of course, proved as much last weekend when United looked desperately short of ideas in attack.

But you would probably bet on Carrick being more likely to find solutions to that particular conundrum than some of the defensive headaches that again reared their head here.

A week after that shock 2-0 defeat to Hull, United were given another scare when Ipswich took advantage of more meek defending to lead and could easily have scored more in that first half.

With a couple of days of the transfer window still remaining, it would feel remiss of United not to add a quality left-back before the deadline passes.

Those 15 minutes in the first half when Abdul Fatawu gave Luke Shaw a torrid time, not least in that moment he raced away from the United defender to cross for Leif Davis to score, should tell United’s hierarchy everything about the risks of not reinforcing in the position.

Ipswich STUN Old Trafford! Leif Davis does superbly to volley past Senne Lammens and give Gary O'Neil's side the lead 💥 pic.twitter.com/sJ0XNf8OiT.

Defensive rebuilding is next summer’s big project but some things cannot wait and that is before we get to some of the issues in the other full-back position, which Ipswich also exploited. Fatawu aside, Daizen Maeda and Davis caused Diogo Dalot and Mbeumo problems down United’s right and the excellent Julio Enciso was a persistent nuisance until the game fell away from Ipswich.

For all the defensive concerns, though, United were exhilarating going forward, especially once they found themselves in front after benefiting from a curious ruling that dictated Harry Maguire’s “accidental” handball in the lead-up to the home team’s second goal was “not punishable” because he did not end up scoring.

In other words, had Maguire himself found the net and not seen his cross-cum-shot deflect in off the Ipswich defender Jacob Greaves, the goal would not have stood.
